The honest compensating control is the far-end **hop-sequence gap** counter: MH assigns `hop_sequence` before handing the datagram to the transport, so a quinn-evicted datagram consumes a hop number and never arrives, and the receiver observes a genuine gap. **Obligation**: state the relationship at *both* entries in `docs/observability/metrics/mh-service.md` — the egress-overflow entry must record that it counts MH's own queue drops only and that quinn may evict silently beneath it, and the hop-gap entry must record that it is the far-end signal for that eviction. Absent the cross-reference each reads as redundant with the other and the pair is a candidate for being "simplified" to one. Task 21's runbook must carry it as an interpretation caveat on the egress-drop signal, because a flat counter during a congestion incident is the actively misleading case, not merely an absent one. **Naming constraint on the same counter, and it is stronger than "blind spot" (raised by @security as S5 at Gate 1 of the same devloop, accepted by @observability as catalog/alert wording)**: the transport below the seam never refuses at all — in production the refusal is produced by MH's own bounded egress queue *above* the seam — so the counter is wholly a property of MH's own queue, and neither its catalog entry nor any alert, dashboard panel or runbook sentence may describe it as observing transport back-pressure. The two facts compose and both are needed: the counter observes only MH's queue (S5), **and** genuine loss occurs beneath it that the counter structurally cannot see (the eviction above). A reader given only the first believes the counter is complete for what it names; given only the second, that it is a degraded version of a transport signal it was never measuring.

Filed 2026-09-08 at story task 19 Gate 2 by @security, after @team-lead observed the file-count change at the commit boundary)**: `crates/dt-guard/src/common/git_changes.rs::get_tracked_files` wraps `git ls-files <pathspec>`, which lists tracked files only. Its four callers — `ts_retained_credentials.rs:824` (`load_in_scope_files`), `no_insecure_browser_flags.rs`, `release_build_profile.rs`, `todo_tracking.rs` — are **whole-tree** scans, so they have NO diff-blindness for existing code. Their blind spot is exactly one shape: **a file that is new and not yet staged does not exist to them.**
  **Observed, not theorised**: at task 19's commit boundary the same guard reported `OK … clean-78-files` unstaged and `99 files` with three violations staged. That control has a has-to-notice blind spot of its own. A guard whose scope silently excludes precisely the code a devloop is writing reports clean for the duration and fires only at the commit boundary, which is the most expensive moment to learn it.

## Infrastructure Validation in Devloops

- [ ] **`dt-guard env-config` discovery is defeated by rustfmt and reports STATUS=OK — the R-34 failure class, second instance (2026-09-03)**: found at the operations review of devloop `2026-09-03-mc-client-media-signaling`; owner `infrastructure` (guard machinery). Required-var discovery is a single-line regex, `MissingEnvVar\("([A-Z_][A-Z0-9_]*)"` (`crates/dt-guard/src/env_config.rs:187`). It cannot span lines, so a rustfmt-wrapped `ConfigError::MissingEnvVar(\n    "VAR".to_string(),\n)` is **invisible to the guard, which then prints `STATUS=OK` for a service whose key is unenforced per-workload** — precisely the "clean verdict for a count that includes what it skipped" that R-34 fixed once already, arriving through a different door.
  **This is not hypothetical and the margin is one character.** `crates/mc-service/src/config.rs:610` is **exactly 100 characters**, rustfmt's default `max_width` with no `rustfmt.toml` in the tree. One more level of nesting, or one more character in the variable name, and the formatter reflows it and silently un-declares the key. The devloop hit this for real on `MC_MAX_RECEIVE_CAPABILITY_DECLARATIONS` and reflowed the call by hand to get back under the limit; a warning comment now sits above it.
  **Why the existing mitigations do not close it**: the tree already knows this hazard in its extract-a-helper form — `511e14fd` records "the presence-check literals are deliberately repeated rather than extracted... a helper would blind it on all thirteen while it kept printing STATUS=OK". Both that note and the new one are comments addressed to a human who is already editing the right lines. The formatter is not reading them, and it acts on line width, not intent. **A guard whose discovery mechanism a routine `cargo fmt` can silently defeat is not a control.**
  **The fix, stated precisely — a naive version of this fires 31 times across the tree and gets disabled.** Most `MissingEnvVar` occurrences legitimately yield no name: measured 2026-09-03, unparseable occurrences are AC 3/5, GC 4/7, MC 13/28, MH 11/24. They are the `MissingEnvVar(String)` enum declaration (4), `Err(ConfigError::MissingEnvVar(v)) if v == "..."` test match arms (24), one `MissingEnvVar(name))` assertion arm, and 2 prose mentions in comments. So the predicate must discriminate structurally, not by allowlist:
  > **Strip comments. Then, if the first non-whitespace character after `MissingEnvVar(` is a double-quote, a valid `[A-Z_][A-Z0-9_]*` name MUST parse out — otherwise hard-fail.**
  Verified against all four `config.rs` files: match arms (`v`), the enum declaration (`String`) and the assertion arm (`name`) are excluded by their first character, while the rustfmt-wrapped case is still caught because its next non-whitespace character is `"`.
  **Second affected guard, same mechanism — and its half is FIXED, which is why this entry now names a class rather than a regex** (added 2026-09-03 by `infrastructure` after @operations root-caused a live Layer-3 red in this same devloop): `crates/dt-guard/src/kustomize.rs::extract_declared_resources` was also line-oriented with no comment strip, so an **inline trailing** comment on a resource entry — `- secret.yaml   # secrets ONLY` — left the entry not ending in `.yaml`, the file was never recorded as declared, and `orphan_manifest` then **reported a listed file as unlisted**. Note the shape of that message: true-shaped, and naming `secret.yaml` — the innocent manifest — rather than the comment that broke the parse. A *standalone* comment line is safe **for R-16 specifically**, because R-16's `- ` anchor excludes it — which is why the long-standing `# service-monitor.yaml NOT listed …` note never tripped it: same character, different position, only one position safe, nothing in the file signalling the difference. **Read that as a property of R-16's anchor, not of comments** (@operations, 2026-09-05, after @infrastructure): stated generally it is false, and stating it generally is exactly what would let a reader skip the sibling below. **Fixed in this devloop** (`split_once('#')` before the suffix test, plus a regression test pinned by an exact-set assertion and verified to fail without the fix), because it was a one-line change in infrastructure's own crate and CLAUDE.md bars parking those here.
  **What remains open is the class, not the two instances.** Three occurrences in one devloop — rustfmt wrapping `MissingEnvVar(`, a doc-comment example registering a phantom var, and this inline comment — share one root: **guard parsers that read lines instead of parsing YAML/Rust, with no comment-stripping step.** Two are `env-config`'s (still open, per the predicate above) and **two** were `kustomize`'s — both closed: R-16's `extract_declared_resources` above, and R-20's `check_dashboard_coverage` 90 lines below it in the same file, **found 2026-09-05 at Gate 3 by @infrastructure running the very sweep this paragraph prescribes**. R-20 is the more instructive of the two because it failed in **both** directions where R-16 failed in one: it shares R-16's inline-comment false positive, but it also has **no `- ` bullet anchor**, so a *standalone* comment naming a dashboard path silently **declared** it — a **fail-open** direction R-16 does not have, in which a genuinely unlisted dashboard merely mentioned in a nearby comment passes R-20 and no finding is raised. That the entry's own prescribed sweep turned up a fourth instance, in a file already fixed once, is the entry's thesis proving itself: **fixing reported instances is what leaves siblings 90 lines away.** **Scoping note so the eventual sweep does not waste effort**: `crates/dt-guard/src/kustomize_tools.rs` has six more `.lines()` loops and is **not** exposed — **it has no file input at all**: zero `read_to_string` in the module, and every parsing entry point (`check_security_context`, `check_empty_secret_data`, `split_yaml_docs`, `run_kubeconform`) takes rendered `kustomize build` output as a `rendered: &str` parameter, while the two surviving `.lines()` loops parse tool *stdout*. Stated as a property of the signatures rather than as "the output is comment-free" (@infrastructure's re-derivation, 2026-09-05): the former is checkable in one grep and cannot quietly stop being true, the latter is a property of `kustomize` that someone could imagine changing. Do not "fix" those; changing them alters behaviour for no reason. **When acted on, sweep for the mechanism rather than fixing reported instances**: every `dt-guard` check that greps source or manifest text for a construct is a candidate, and the tell is a `.lines()` loop with a suffix or prefix test and no `#`/`//` handling. Fixing them one incident at a time is how three instances reached one devloop.
 Multi-line tolerance falls out for free, so this subsumes "match across lines" rather than needing it as a separate step. **The comment-stripping step also closes the inverse defect found in the same pass** — a `MissingEnvVar("...")` example inside a doc comment registered a phantom required var named `KEY` — so one rule fixes both the false negative and the false positive. Credit: predicate from `infrastructure`, refining a naive "fail on anything unparseable" that would have been disabled within a week. A fuller fix (parse `config.rs` as Rust) remains available but is not needed for this.
  **The class is wider than "guards parse lines", and the evidence for that arrived by the mechanism biting the fix itself (@infrastructure, 2026-09-04, while landing the `kustomize` half above).** Verifying the new regression test meant removing the fix to confirm the test would fail — done with a single-line replace. The test **passed**, which was very nearly logged as "verified". The replace had matched nothing: `cargo fmt` had already reflowed the one-liner across four lines, so the line-oriented pattern found no target and silently changed nothing. Redone with a pattern that asserts it applied, after which the control failed correctly. **So the generalisation is: any line-oriented match over formatted source is unsafe — including the ones we write to check our own work.** A verification step that can pass vacuously converts an unproven control into an apparently-proven one, which is strictly worse than no verification, and it is the same defect this devloop already recorded against a racing premise assertion in `media_client_signaling_integration.rs`. **Whoever acts on this entry must therefore verify the fix with a step that asserts its own precondition** (the edit applied, the pattern matched), not merely that the test flipped colour. Framing credited to @operations, incident to @infrastructure.

- [ ] **`run-story.test.sh`'s containment check reports a THIRD-PARTY writer as this suite's own breach, reddening Layer 3 in any multi-agent devloop — NOT a flake (owner `infrastructure`, validation machinery; filed 2026-09-04 by @operations, re-diagnosed and merged 2026-09-05 by @operations + @infrastructure at Gate 3 of `docs/devloop-outputs/2026-09-03-mc-client-media-signaling/`; carries infrastructure's accepted I-E deferral)**: `./scripts/layer3.sh` reports `STATUS=FAIL REASON=run-story-selftest-failed` → `LAYER=3 RESULT=FAIL` while `bash scripts/workflow/run-story.test.sh` standalone passes 290/290, whenever another agent writes to `/work` during the run. Guards themselves are clean in the same runs (`run-guards.sh` → 40/40, rc 0, `Failed (violations): 0`), so the only evidence in a filtered log is the summary line.

  **This entry was originally filed as "a ~30%-flaky gate" with a candidates list. That framing was wrong and is retracted, not softened.** Two separate errors produced it, both worth keeping because they are the same error: (1) @operations reasoned from the aggregate `REASON=` line, which cannot distinguish a containment abort from a failing case, and concluded "flake"; the *captured* output names the cause outright — `run-story.test.sh: CONTAINMENT-FAILURE — the REAL repository at /work changed during this run.` (2) The original entry then listed "tree mutation during the run" as **ruled out**. It is the cause. **Reasoning about an anonymous failure is what produced a wrong exclusion**, which is exactly the defect the "first diagnostic step" below already named — the entry contained its own refutation and neither of us read it that way for a day. The former candidates (a) `DEVLOOP_TMP` seam contention, (b) timing sensitivity, (c) a `$?`/pipefail mistranslation are **dropped**: they were ghosts inferred from a filtered status.

  **The mechanism, re-derived from source rather than inferred.** The suite has a deliberate four-token closed vocabulary (`run-story.test.sh` header) that already tries to separate concurrency from a real breach: `NOT-QUIESCENT` (tree already moving at pre-flight → refuse up front), `CONTAINMENT-UNREADABLE` (git health), `CONTAINMENT-UNVERIFIED` (changed AND still moving → attribute nothing), `CONTAINMENT-FAILURE` (changed and post-state **stable**, so one actor explains it → real breach). The discriminator between the last two is **temporal, not attributive**: it re-samples and asks "is the tree still moving *now*", using stability as a proxy for "the writer was me". **The limit is already written down in the file** — *"a writer that stops before the re-sample looks stable and is reported as a containment failure — over-reporting, the safe direction. OBSERVED 2026-08-17"* — so this is at least the third observation, honestly stated by its author, not a new discovery.

  **What is genuinely stale is the trigger list, and that is the actionable half (@infrastructure).** The comment names `cargo fmt` in the same command as the plausible trigger and prescribes **"RE-RUN THE SUITE ALONE BEFORE INVESTIGATING"** — advice that assumes the concurrent writer is *the operator's own process*. In a multi-agent Gate 3 the writer is another agent, "run it alone" is not something the runner can arrange, and **bursty** writes make the stable-post-state case the normal outcome rather than the corner one.

  **Why the `NOT-QUIESCENT` pre-flight does not save us, which is where the leverage actually is.** The pre-flight takes two **back-to-back** samples with no sleep (deliberately — it must not add wall-clock to an always-run layer), so its detection window is tens of milliseconds while the **exposure window is the entire run**. An agent doing edit/verify cycles is bursty, not continuous: it passes a narrow pre-flight, writes during the wide run, and stops before the post re-sample. **Widening the pre-flight is not the fix either** — it trades an always-run layer's latency for a probabilistic guess. The asymmetry between the two windows is the defect, not either window's size.

  **DO NOT "fix" this by narrowing the comparison.** The source says so at the `CONTAINMENT-FAILURE` branch — *"The comparison is deliberately NOT narrowed to make this quiet — the three captures stay, because narrowing is what would make the proof worthless"* — and that is the whole reason infrastructure deferred rather than patching it (see below). The promising direction is to make the discriminator **attributive rather than temporal** — but the path set must be derived from the write paths, and **the obvious formulation is backwards in the direction that matters.**

  **The trap, recorded because the first draft of this paragraph fell into it (@operations, corrected by @infrastructure, 2026-09-05).** It is tempting to write "a delta confined to `docs/**` cannot be this suite". That is **exactly wrong, and it fails silently toward under-reporting on the canonical breach.** `dt-story` is the REAL binary via the `DT_STORY` seam and `git` is real by design (the suite header: containment "must be tested against the tool that actually resolves upward"), the suite drives the manifest-**writing** verbs `complete` / `escalate` / `add-task`, and `run-story.sh`'s trust-boundary guard says it outright: *"`DT_STORY` in particular selects the binary that runs 'complete'/'escalate' **against the real manifest**."* Story manifests live in **`docs/user-stories/*.md`**. So a breach — a seam root that resolves upward into the real clone — writes precisely into `docs/**`. A `docs/**` exemption would flip that verdict from breach to not-a-breach on a green run.

  **The sound form is the inverse: enumerate what the suite can reach ON A BREACH, and attribute elsewhere only a delta touching nothing in that set.** Derived from the write paths rather than eyeballed — there are exactly two in the crate: (1) the story markdown, via `main.rs::save` → `engine::rewrite_story` → `engine::write_atomic` (a `NamedTempFile` + `persist` over the target), which under a breach lands in `docs/user-stories/**`; and (2) the escalation JSON sidecar written by the `escalate` arm to its `--escalation-out` path. `dt-story` shells no `git` (zero `Command::new` in the crate), so `.git` mutation is `run-story.sh`'s commit path, not the binary's. **Reachable set: `docs/user-stories/**`, the escalation-out path, and whatever `run-story.sh`'s commit path touches.** Everything else — `crates/**`, `infra/**`, `docs/runbooks/**`, `docs/TODO.md` — is outside it, which covers every write the reviewers actually made during the observed runs. **A delta touching `docs/user-stories/**` stays a breach verdict regardless of timing.**

  **Second trap, the mirror image of the first, and it defeats path-keying from the opposite side (@infrastructure, 2026-09-05).** The runner's completion path is `git add "$STORY_FILE"` followed by `git commit --quiet --amend --no-edit`, and **an amend commits whatever is already in the index**, not only what that `git add` staged. Committing *removes* files from `status --porcelain` and from `diff HEAD` — so a commit-path breach makes the path delta **shrink**, potentially to empty. An implementer keying attribution on "which paths appear in the delta" would see *fewer* suspicious paths after a breach than before and exempt it. The first trap silences a breach by naming an innocent-looking path; this one silences it by making the path set look empty. **Both defeat a filter that only asks which paths changed.**

  **Therefore: test the HEAD field FIRST, and a moved HEAD is a breach verdict regardless of the path delta.** The capture is `HEAD|sha256(status --porcelain)|sha256(diff HEAD)`, so a commit-path breach *is* detected today — the first field moves — but only because the composite string differs, which is exactly the property a path-based refinement would discard. The HEAD test must run **before** any path-based exemption, not alongside it.

  **The worst consequence needs no staged files at all: the amend lands on the loop's own rollback anchor (@infrastructure, 2026-09-05).** A devloop's `main.md` records a **Start Commit** and its Rollback Procedure says `git reset --hard {start_commit}`. While a loop's work is uncommitted, **HEAD *is* that anchor** — verified on this loop: `git rev-parse HEAD` and the recorded Start Commit are both `1d755455`. So a commit-path breach runs `git commit --quiet --amend --no-edit` **onto the exact commit the documented recovery procedure tells you to reset to**, rewriting the recovery target. This is unconditional: it holds with a completely empty index, and it is outside the case the runner's authors reasoned about — `run-story.sh`'s canary comment establishes that `$RUN_DIR` lives under `DEVLOOP_TMP`, "outside the work tree, so `git add` and the amend below cannot sweep it", which is an argument about what gets swept **into** the commit and says nothing about what the commit **replaces**.

  **Secondary, and conditional rather than usual**: because the amend commits the **index** and not only the `git add`ed manifest, anything else staged at that moment is swept into the same commit. A mid-review tree *can* carry staged work, so the blast radius is not bounded by what the suite writes. **Stated as a conditional deliberately** — an earlier revision of this entry asserted staged work was "the normal state of a devloop mid-Gate-3" and offered this loop as the worked example; measured, `git diff --cached --name-only` was **empty**, so the example did not support the claim. The mechanism is structural and holds; the frequency was asserted without measuring, and the sentence a reader will never re-derive is exactly the one that must not be.

  **So HEAD-first ordering is now argued from three independent directions**, which is why it is a hard requirement and not a preference: a path-keyed filter can be handed innocent-looking paths (the `docs/**` trap above), sees the delta **shrink** on a commit-path breach (the trap above that), and — decisively — **the most damaged artifact is not in the path delta at all; it is the commit the delta is measured against.** `sha256(diff HEAD)` changing is the symptom; HEAD having been rewritten is the injury. Test the HEAD field before any path-based exemption, and never let a path filter reach a verdict that a moved HEAD would have called a breach.

  That version removes the timing race from the safety verdict *and* keeps the canonical breach loud, which is the property the temporal discriminator lacks. **Note the set is what the suite could write IF A GUARD FAILED, not what it writes today**: B1 (`SEAM-ROOT-NOT-OWN-TOPLEVEL`, exit 2, no filesystem writes) is refused up front precisely so this never happens — the containment check is the backstop for that refusal failing, so its attribution set must be derived from the write paths, not from observed behaviour. It is a design change needing its own validation, which is why it is deferred and not a one-liner.

  **Accepted deferral (infrastructure's I-E; accepted by @operations, ratified by @team-lead).** `scripts/workflow/run-story.test.sh` is outside the `2026-09-03-mc-client-media-signaling` changeset, and the correct predicate has to distinguish the suite's own writes from a third party's — where the cheap version is to relax a containment control, which is the one thing this file must not do. Fix-now cost (design + its own test cycle + the risk of weakening a safety gate) exceeds fix-later cost. **The interim mitigation is operational, not code**: run the authority `layer-all.sh` against a **quiescent** tree — reviewers idle, no pending writes. That is now the operative procedure rather than a workaround.

  **Why the interim mitigation is not sufficient long-term**: it depends on a human judgement (is the tree quiescent?) made by the person most motivated to answer "yes", and this file's own precedent says **a control that depends on an optional judgement is not a control**. Worse, the failure is bidirectional: a correct containment abort reads as a regression, and — the dangerous direction — **a real regression gets waved off as "that flake"**, which the original framing of this very entry would have licensed.

  **Related, deliberately NOT merged**: the `run_and_emit` rc→enum collapse under §Polyglot Pipeline Follow-ups (ADR-0033 Wave 1 #1), which records @code-reviewer's CQ-16 instance of this same collision from the *other* direction — a containment exit 2 collapsing to `STATUS=FAIL` → rc 1 → a task escalated against a clean diff. The source comment at the discriminator names it as a separate filed follow-up (*"The rc-1 collapse itself is @paired-infrastructure's filed follow-up; this stops feeding it a false signal"*), and they are two defects that compound rather than one filed twice: this entry is *why the wrong verdict is produced*, that one is *why the wrong verdict is amplified into an escalation*. Fixing either alone leaves a real hole. Cross-referenced rather than concatenated, per this file's own precedent that a merge decision needs judgement.

  **Defer trigger**: any edit to `scripts/workflow/run-story.test.sh` or its `layer3.sh` invocation; or the first time this verdict is dismissed as a flake on a tree that was genuinely quiescent. **Do not budget for a loop-until-fail harness** — the earlier entry recommended one on the flake premise, and it is wasted effort now that the mechanism is known and deterministic given a concurrent writer. Reproduce it directly: write to the tree mid-run and stop before the re-sample.

- [ ] **Layer 7 cannot deploy an `infra/services/**` change — `rebuild-all` applies the image but never the manifests, and the infra-change detector watches `infra/kind/` only (2026-09-03)**: spun out by `infrastructure` at Gate 3 of devloop `2026-09-03-mc-client-media-signaling`; owner `infrastructure` (validation + devloop-helper machinery). **Mechanism, three files.** (1) `scripts/layer7.sh:492` phase 1c runs `"$DEV_CLUSTER" rebuild-all`. (2) `crates/devloop-helper/src/commands.rs:1084-1113` — `cmd_rebuild` is *build image → `load_image_to_kind` → `restart_deployment`*, with **no manifest apply**; the apply lives only in `cmd_deploy` (`commands.rs:1128-1163`, which shells `setup.sh --yes --skip-build --only <svc>` → `kubectl apply -k` on the Kind overlay). (3) `scripts/layer7.sh:476` — the one manifest-refresh arm is `if diff_touches_path "infra/kind/"`, and its response is a full teardown + setup. **`infra/services/**` is watched by nothing.** So a diff that changes a service ConfigMap or Deployment and then runs Layer 7 against a warm cluster deploys the **new image against the old ConfigMap and old pod template, by construction, every time** — the manifest half of the diff is never validated, and Layer 7 nonetheless reports on it.
  **Observed live, and the symptom pointed at the wrong artifact.** Gate 2 of that devloop: `dev-cluster setup` failed with `port allocation failed: port 24500 (prometheus) is already in use`, which was downstream noise — setup only re-ran *because* `mc-0`/`mc-1` were already in `CrashLoopBackOff` on `MissingEnvVar("MC_MAX_RECEIVE_SLOTS")`, the new image having met the stale in-cluster ConfigMap. A port-conflict message for a config-deployment defect is close to the worst available first clue; the recovery is written up in `docs/runbooks/mc-deployment.md` §Config-failure triage, but the *cause* is this gap and no document names it.
  **This will recur for every future devloop touching `infra/services/**`, and it gets worse as more keys become required.** The `MC_*`/`MH_*` fail-loud-required convention (`511e14fd`, and the five ADR-0036 keys here) is correct and should stay; its cost is that a stale ConfigMap is now a two-pod outage rather than a silent misconfiguration, which makes an undeployable manifest change a hard stop instead of a shrug.
  **The fix is NOT to widen the `infra/kind/` predicate** — teardown + setup is a several-minute response to what needs a `kubectl apply -k`, and it would make every manifest one-liner pay full cluster bring-up. Add a **third arm** between (b) and (c) in `scripts/layer7.sh`: on `diff_touches_path "infra/services/"`, map each changed `infra/services/<svc>/` prefix to its service and run `"$DEV_CLUSTER" deploy <svc>` before `rebuild-all`. Ordering matters — apply manifests first, then rebuild/restart, so the restart picks up the new pod template in one roll rather than two. **Alternative worth weighing first**: fold the apply into `cmd_rebuild` itself, so `rebuild` means "make the cluster run my current tree" for manifests as well as images. That is the more honest verb and removes the whole class rather than one call site, but it changes shared devloop-tool semantics used by every loop and by `dev-cluster` interactively, so it needs the ADR-0030 owner's ruling, not a drive-by.
  **Test surface, which is why this is task-sized and not a fold-in**: `scripts/layer7.test.sh` needs a case asserting the new arm fires on an `infra/services/` diff and does *not* fire on an unrelated one, plus a case pinning the apply-before-rebuild ordering; the helper side needs coverage in the `devloop-helper` suite if the `cmd_rebuild` option is taken. Not doable inside a service devloop: shared validation machinery, ADR-0024 §6.3.
  **Sibling, same root**: the `dt-guard env-config` rustfmt entry immediately above. That one is "the guard cannot see a required key"; this one is "the pipeline cannot deploy the manifest that supplies it." Both let Layer 3/7 print green over an MC that would not start.

So on a fresh namespace `apply -k` yields four pods that cannot start, and nothing in the declarative tree says why.

Its failure is also a **different first step** from the required-key CrashLoop the banner is about: a missing TLS Secret fails the *file*-existence check, not the env check, so the responder should be looking at the `mc-tls` volume and `kubectl get secret mc-service-tls`, not at the ConfigMap. `operations` has documented that distinction in `docs/runbooks/mc-deployment.md` §Kubernetes Secrets; this entry is the infrastructure half — the runbook explains the symptom, nothing removes the cause.
  **Named operations follow-up, the MH runbook half (owner: `operations`; TRIGGER: the next devloop touching `docs/runbooks/mh-deployment.md`, or this entry being acted on — whichever is first).** The symptom is documented for **MC only**. `docs/runbooks/mh-deployment.md` currently contains **zero** occurrences of `mh-service-tls`, `mh-tls` or `MH_TLS`, so the identical MH failure — `apply -k`, four unstartable pods, `FailedMount` on the `mh-tls` volume — has no operator-facing home at all. **The symptom this bullet originally named was wrong, and it is corrected here rather than left standing because this bullet is a WORK ORDER** (@operations, 2026-09-05, after @infrastructure): it said "cert *file*-existence check", which would have been copied straight into an operator-facing runbook as the first step. Cite `infra/services/mh-service/kustomization.yaml`, which now carries the corrected wording, rather than re-deriving it. Recorded as a specific named sibling rather than left as "out of scope": it is one mechanism with one owner, and the MC half is only documented because this devloop happened to touch an MC runbook hunk. **Not folded into the MC diff** because `mh-deployment.md` is outside this changeset with no other hunk in it, so adding it means a further plan-table row for a pre-existing gap in a service this devloop does not otherwise touch. **But note precisely what that leaves, because it is this file's own OPS-11 mechanism one more time**: the diff *does* touch `docs/runbooks/mh-incident-response.md` (the MC-topology cross-reference), so the MH runbook **set** ships half-corrected — one MH runbook updated by this loop, its sibling untouched and silent on a failure mode the MC runbooks now document in detail. A reader who checks `mh-incident-response.md`, finds it current, and infers the MH runbooks were reviewed will conclude wrongly. That asymmetry, not the missing paragraph, is the reason this follow-up needs a trigger rather than a backlog slot. The fix is ~12 lines mirroring `mc-deployment.md` §Kubernetes Secrets, and the `kustomization.yaml` comment landed here is what a reader editing the manifests will hit meanwhile. **When acted on, write the SET rather than the third row.** There are now three distinct startup-config signals — `FailedMount` (Secret absent, mount blocked), `CreateContainerConfigError` (ConfigMap key absent, container never ran) and `CrashLoopBackOff` (stale pod template, process started and exited) — and the generalisation is worth more to a responder than any one row: **`kubectl logs` is empty or misleading for all three**, so the standard first reflex is wrong every time, and `kubectl describe pod` is what names the artifact in the first two. Rejected on that ground, not on cost. The banner is scoped to the five required keys and should stay scoped.

The real options each need a decision this devloop could not make — (a) a `secretGenerator` over the output of `scripts/generate-dev-certs.sh`, which keeps material out of git but only works where those files exist; (b) sealed-secrets / External Secrets, which is a new cluster dependency; (c) keep it imperative and make the *declarative* tree state the prerequisite so `apply -k` fails loudly rather than producing four unstartable pods. **Interim, landed in this devloop**: a comment in both `kustomization.yaml` files naming the imperative creator, following the convention already set there by `# service-monitor.yaml NOT listed — requires Prometheus Operator CRD`. That is navigation, not a control, and does not close this entry.
  **Defer trigger**: any work on cluster bootstrap outside `setup.sh` (CI, a second environment, production), or the next devloop touching `infra/services/{mc,mh}-service/secret.yaml`. Until then `setup.sh` is the only supported bootstrap and it does the right thing.

The total-by-construction alternative is a compile-time assertion on the **effective cfg**:

    ```rust
    #[cfg(all(feature = "release-artifact", debug_assertions))]
    compile_error!("release artifact built with debug_assertions enabled");
    ```

  with the service Dockerfiles passing `--features release-artifact`. That catches all seven channels *and* ones nobody has enumerated — §11's own technique, applied to the premise instead of to the tracing feature: "a compile error has nothing to notice." **Complement, not replacement**: the guard catches the source change early, legibly, across all four services at review time and can say *which* channel broke; the `cfg` assertion catches the artifact totally but can only say "compile error". - [ ] **`producer | grep -q` under `set -o pipefail` is a latent false-negative class — swept and counted, NOT fixed** (surfaced 2026-08-15 at Gate 3 by @infrastructure while fixing one instance in `infra/kind/scripts/setup.sh:provision_run_org()`; generalisation prompted by @test; devloop `docs/devloop-outputs/2026-08-15-layer7-per-run-org/`). **Mechanism**: `grep -q` exits at the FIRST match and closes the pipe; if the producer has more to write it takes SIGPIPE (141) and `pipefail` makes the **whole pipeline non-zero even though the pattern WAS found**. Reachability is a function of (producer's stdout buffer) vs (position of the match), so it is invisible on small inputs and appears as the input grows — the worst possible discovery curve for a gate. This is the sibling of the `find | head` / `tr | head` trap already documented at `scripts/workflow/run-story.sh:748-776`; that one is about the producer *failing*, this one is about the producer *succeeding and being cut off*.
  **Measured in this repo, today** (not theoretical): `git ls-files | grep -qxF <first-path>` false-negatives against this repo right now (71 KB of output, needle on line 1); with the needle on the LAST line it passes, which is the tell that the match position is half the mechanism. Independently reproduced by @test from a **script file** rather than an agent Bash shell, per this devloop's own §Issues #2 lesson.
  **TWO DISTINCT MECHANISMS — do not collapse them, they imply different regression tests** (corrected 2026-08-15 by @test, re-measured independently by @infrastructure; earlier drafts of this entry described only the first and framed it as a clean size threshold, which was one sample per point and wrong in both directions):
  - **(a) Incremental producer** (`git ls-files`, `git show --name-only`, `kubectl`, shell loops) — a **scheduler RACE**. It fires well below the pipe buffer and never becomes a clean threshold. 30 runs/point, needle on line 1: `kubectl config get-contexts` 100 contexts **2/30**, 200 **18/30**, 300 **29/30**, 3000 **30/30**; `git show --name-only` N=80 **0/30**, N=200 **8/30**, N=300 **27/30**, N=400 **29/30**.
  - **(b) `cat`-backed producer** — `__changed_files()` is `cat "$cache"` (`_changed_helpers.sh:39-43`), a plain file read, which makes reproduction **byte-driven**. But it is *not* cleanly deterministic at the buffer boundary either: 20 runs/point over a synthetic cache, needle on line 1, `grep -qxF` consumer — 24 KB **0/20**, 48 KB **0/20**, 72 KB **1/20**, 77 KB **0/20**, 96 KB **1/20**, 144 KB **20/20**. So there is an intermittent band around the pipe buffer and determinism only well above it. **Neither mechanism licenses a "safe under N" claim** — and this is the one line to keep when the numbers above drift, because it is the instruction, not the data.
  **METHODOLOGICAL WARNING, earned the hard way — read before trusting any number in this entry.** Over the drafting of *this single entry* a size claim was flattened into a threshold **three times**, and every one was wrong: "the detector stops firing on any commit touching ~80+ files" (@infrastructure; actually 0/30 at N=80), "deterministic at ~68 KB" (@test; actually an intermittent band), and "no arrangement of that gate holds" (@test; actually a real conditional rescue in the middle band). Each was caught only by **re-running at more than one sample per point**, and the third was written *after* its author had authored the correction for the second — knowing the failure mode did not prevent repeating it. Two independent reviewers, three instances, one entry. So: every number here is a distribution, not a step; single-sample measurements of SIGPIPE races are worthless; and any future edit that turns one of these bands back into a threshold is reintroducing the defect the entry is about.
  **CONSUMER LANDSCAPE UPDATE (2026-08-20, validation-run-all devloop) — the bug and the file are UNCHANGED and STILL LIVE; only which consumers are exposed shifted.** `_changed_helpers.sh` stays; `:54`/`:66`/`:100` are untouched. But the per-lang `changed.sh` classifiers (`rust/changed.sh:6`, `ts/changed.sh:7`) that this entry cites as consumers were **DELETED** when the skip-if-untouched policy was retired (ADR-0033 §2/§3). Consequences to re-read accordingly: (1) the "big Rust change silently skips compile/fmt/clippy/test" scenario below is **OBSOLETE** — those language layers now **always-run** regardless of any diff predicate, so a `diff_touches_path` false-negative can no longer skip them. (2) The **security-critical consequence is UNCHANGED and remains the whole point**: the surviving `:66`/`diff_touches_root_files` + `diff_touches_glob` consumers are `_audit_gate.sh` (the **dependency audit gate**) — a false-negative there still silently skips the security audit with a green pipeline. (3) `diff_touches_path` (`:54`) now has one surviving consumer, `layer7.sh` Phase-1b's `diff_touches_path "infra/kind/"` cluster-rebuild check — a false-negative there runs the suite against a **stale cluster**. Fix `:54`/`:66` per the prescribed shape below regardless; the audit-gate exposure is why this stays high-priority. The measured bands are preserved verbatim below for the record; read the `rust/changed.sh` mentions as historical.
  **The sharp remaining sites, all gate logic, all under `set -euo pipefail`, owner `operations`:**
  - `scripts/lang/_changed_helpers.sh:54` — `diff_touches_path()`'s `__changed_files | awk 'index($0,p)==1 { found=1; exit }'`. **THE WORST SITE IN THE REPO, and it was missed by the first two passes of this entry** (found by @test): `awk … exit` is an early-exit consumer exactly like `grep -q`, and it reproduces where the others do not — 20/20 false negatives from ~72 KB up, versus `grep -qxF`'s 1/20 at the same size. **The composite consequence is worse than either predicate alone, and it has THREE BANDS — do not flatten it in either direction.** `scripts/lang/rust/changed.sh:6` is `diff_touches_path "crates/" || diff_touches_root_files "Cargo.toml" "Cargo.lock" "rust-toolchain.toml"`, so the `||` reads as a safety net. Measured on a faithful replica and confirmed by @test against the real script with a real cache file, 20 runs/point, needle at git-realistic position:
    - **< ~1500 changed files (~72 KB)** — both branches fine (pure-`crates/` N=100 and N=1000: 0/20).
    - **~1500–2500 files** — `diff_touches_path` fails **20/20**, and the fallback rescues the run **only if a root manifest is in the changeset**. A pure-`crates/` changeset here is already **skipped 20/20 at N=2000 (92 KB)** — and that is the common shape of a large Rust change. With `Cargo.toml` also touched, N=2000 recovers 20/20 (`diff_touches_root_files` 0/20 at that size).
    - **> ~3000 files (~138 KB)** — **both branches fail 20/20 regardless**; N=3000 and N=4000 classify Rust as untouched even with `Cargo.toml` in the diff. At this size no arrangement of the gate holds.
    So the `||` is not a degraded safety net — it is a **second independent instance of the same bug** that merely fails later, and @test's `Cargo.lock`/`rust-toolchain.toml` finding below removes the only operands that could have sorted late enough to survive. (An earlier draft of this bullet said the fallback simply "returns 1 too"; @test then measured it failing at N=4000 and generalised to "no arrangement holds". Both overshoot: the middle band is a real, conditional rescue. Recorded precisely because a band structure nobody would guess is exactly what makes this gate's behaviour untrustworthy — it is size-dependent, and the dependence is invisible.)
    The trap is self-reinforcing: the changeset must be large to fire, and a large Rust changeset is precisely a pure-`crates/` one, so **the bigger the Rust change, the more certainly its validation is skipped**. **Severity in the language of the thing protected: on a large Rust changeset, compile / fmt / clippy / test AND the Rust dependency audit are all skipped, silently, with the pipeline green.** That is "fail loudly, never mask" inverted, measured rather than argued. Fix `:54` first.
  - `scripts/lang/_changed_helpers.sh:66` — `diff_touches_root_files()`'s `__changed_files | grep -qxF -- "$f"`. Same class, less exposed than `:54` (intermittent from ~72 KB, deterministic only ~144 KB ≈ 3000 changed files), but the blast radius is the widest (@test): the predicate feeds `scripts/lang/_audit_gate.sh:101,116` — the **dependency audit gate** — as well as `scripts/lang/rust/changed.sh:6` and `scripts/lang/ts/changed.sh:7`. A false negative on the Rust needle therefore **silently skips the security audit**, with a green pipeline. Exposure is asymmetric and measurable: `Cargo.toml` sorts at position **54 of 1395** tracked paths (uppercase sorts before lowercase, so it is in the first 4% of any changeset containing it — maximum SIGPIPE exposure), while `pnpm-lock.yaml` sorts at **1274 of 1395**, so the TS half is far less exposed. **`diff_touches_root_files` has ZERO direct self-test coverage** — `scripts/lang/_changed_helpers.test.sh`'s own header says it is "focused on `diff_touches_glob`" and calls that sibling "security-load-bearing — a wrong match/skip = wrong audit run/skip", while leaving this one untested. Scope the regression test to the **audit gate**, not merely to layer skipping.
  - **Compounding, and it makes the position-54 point decisive** (@test's separate finding, verified): **`Cargo.lock` is gitignored** (`.gitignore:5`; `git ls-files --error-unmatch Cargo.lock` → not tracked) and **`rust-toolchain.toml` does not exist** in this repo. So of `diff_touches_root_files "Cargo.toml" "Cargo.lock" "rust-toolchain.toml"`, **exactly one operand can ever match — `Cargo.toml`, the one at sort position 54 of 1395, i.e. worst-case needle position.** There is no second operand to fall back on. Worse, `scripts/lang/_audit_gate.test.sh:39` asserts `"rust: Cargo.lock changed -> run"`, i.e. it certifies coverage on an input the pipeline **cannot produce** — a test that passes on an impossible input rather than one that cannot fail. Different species from the vacuous-pass bugs this devloop fixed, same family. Include in the operations devloop's scope: either track `Cargo.lock` (it is a binary/application workspace, so committing it is the conventional call and would also make the audit gate mean what its test claims) or drop the dead operands and fix the test. **A third consequence, surfaced 2026-09-02 at Gate 3 of `docs/devloop-outputs/2026-09-02-mh-register-meeting-policy-apply/` (@security, concurred by @operations)**: because the on-disk lock carries real registry checksums, a reviewer clearing a dependency addition will read one and write "checksum-pinned at `Cargo.lock:<n>`" as evidence — which happened at that devloop's Gate 1 and had to be corrected at Gate 3. Cargo still verifies checksums against the registry index at build time, so the exposure is **version drift inside the declared semver range across environments**, not tampering; the durable evidence for a dependency addition is the Layer-6 dep-change gate firing (`scripts/lang/_audit_gate.sh:audit_dep_changed_rust`, which triggers on `Cargo.toml` paths and is unaffected by the lock being untracked), never a lock line. Filed here rather than as a new §Supply Chain entry because the fact is already tracked in two places and a third copy would be the drift this file exists to prevent.
  - `scripts/workflow/run-story.sh:1212` — `git show HEAD --format= --name-only | grep -q '^audit-suppressions\.toml$'`. `audit-suppressions.toml` sorts very early in git's path order (only dotfile dirs precede it), so the needle is near line 1 — the worst position. Reproduction rate rises with commit size per the race numbers above (0/30 at 80 files, 29/30 at 400); it never becomes a clean threshold.
  **Lower-risk siblings, assessed rather than assumed** (owner `infrastructure`, mine; enumerated so nobody re-derives the list): `infra/kind/scripts/setup.sh:355,1365` and `infra/devloop/devloop.sh:653` (`kind get clusters | grep -q` — a handful of lines, one write; and a false negative leads to a loud `kind create cluster` failure, not a silent pass); `infra/kind/scripts/setup.sh:393` (`kubectl get pods -l k8s-app=calico-node | grep -q calico-node` — small label-selected output, match is NOT on line 1, and it sits in a retry loop so a spurious miss costs one iteration); `infra/devloop/devloop.sh:357,406` and `scripts/lang/rust/test.sh:65` (`podman ps --format | grep -q '^name$'` — reachable at ~100+ running containers, consequence is starting a duplicate container, i.e. visibly wrong rather than silently green). Also in the sweep: `scripts/lang/ts/audit.sh:107`, `scripts/dev-web.sh:269,271`, `scripts/test-oauth-integration.sh:41,43,54,112` (`echo "$KUBECTL_LOGS" | grep -q` — a builtin producer with a potentially large log variable, same class).
  **Why not fixed in the R-7 diff**: cross-owner (all three sharp sites are `operations`-owned validation-pipeline gate logic → Domain-judgment under ADR-0024 §6.3, routes to owner-implements), and each site needs its own reachability measurement plus a regression test, which is its own test surface. Fixing them blind by mechanical rewrite is exactly the change-pattern §6.2 forbids classifying as Mechanical.
  **Fix shape — THE PRECEDENT ALREADY SHIPS IN THE SAME FILE, three functions down** (@test). `diff_touches_glob()` at `_changed_helpers.sh:100` measures **0/20 at every size tested, up to 144 KB**, because it reads via **process substitution** — `while IFS= read -r line; do … return 0; done < <(__changed_files)` — so there is no pipe, and an early `return` cannot become a producer SIGPIPE. The operations devloop does not need to invent a shape: **make `:54` and `:66` look like `:100`.** That is more convincing than a recipe because it already ships and already passes, and it keeps the three predicates in one idiom instead of two. Where process substitution does not fit, read into a variable and match with a herestring (`x="$(producer)" || x=""; grep -qxF "$needle" <<<"$x"` — the shape used for the `setup.sh` fix); only where streaming genuinely matters, `producer | grep -qxF … || rc=$?` with the 141 case handled explicitly.
  **REGRESSION-TEST SHAPE IS PRESCRIBED, and a count-based repro MUST NOT SHIP** (@test). An earlier draft of this entry said "drive a producer past its buffer"; per the race numbers above that yields a test which fails to reproduce the bug ~1 run in 30 even at N=400 — a test that cannot be trusted to have caught anything, under ADR-0028's zero-retry policy. That is this devloop's own vacuous-pass class one level up. Use a producer that **blocks after emitting the match**, which forces the SIGPIPE window open with certainty and needs no size tuning: `{ printf 'needle\n'; sleep 0.2; printf 'more\n'; } | grep -q '^needle$'` — verified **30/30** rc=141, versus 2/30–29/30 for every count-based driver. Use a blocking read rather than `sleep` to keep it at ~0s. **Schedule as an operations devloop**; the `infrastructure`-owned siblings above ride along or are explicitly declined with the reasoning already recorded here. Owner: operations (lead), infrastructure (siblings).

- [ ] **Deploy-step validation**: Devloops that modify K8s manifests, kustomization files, setup.sh, or other deploy infrastructure currently have no way to validate their changes actually work — issues like Kustomize path restrictions, postgres security context incompatibilities, and selector mutation only surface when running `setup.sh` against a real cluster. Need to figure out how to incorporate deploy validation into the devloop workflow (e.g., `kustomize build` dry-run, Kind cluster in CI, or a lightweight deploy-test step).

- [ ] **absorb-devloop.sh: detect duplicate tracking-table rows after cherry-pick** (surfaced 2026-06-22 after many manual dedup commits during the post-PR-58 debt-repayment wave): `.gitattributes` sets `docs/user-stories/*.md merge=union` so parallel devloops appending different tracking rows don't conflict. But when a devloop modifies an existing row IN-PLACE (the Step 8 Pending→Completed flip) AND the host has made any intervening edit to user-story.md between clone-creation and absorb, the cherry-pick context drifts and `union-merge` silently keeps BOTH the original Pending row AND the new Completed row instead of replacing. The result is a duplicate row that the operator has to spot and manually remove every absorb. Observed at #46/#47/#48/#49/#52/#9/#10 (every absorb that landed after an intervening host edit) but NOT at #50/#54/#55 (no intervening host edit between clone-create and absorb). Fix: post-cherry-pick scan in `infra/devloop/absorb-devloop.sh` for duplicate task-ID rows in the affected user-story file (e.g., `awk -F'|' '/^\| [0-9]+ \|/ {print $2}' | sort | uniq -d`); if any appear, exit non-zero with a clear message naming the duplicated IDs so the operator can dedup before the absorb completes — same "refuse to silently apply a bad resolution" discipline the script already has for other conflict classes. Strictly an after-the-fact detector, not a preventer, but removes the silent-bad-resolution failure mode. Same dupe class probably lurks for `docs/TODO.md` (also `merge=union`) — we just haven't seen the host edit TODO.md between clone-create and absorb yet. **Update 2026-08-17**: the tracking table this was filed against was retired by the story-runner-hardening story, but the hazard moved rather than closed — the `dt-story` manifest now lives in the same `merge=union` file with the same in-place flip (`status: pending` → `status: completed`, plus a new `slug:` line). It should now fail *loudly* rather than silently, since duplicate keys in one YAML mapping do not parse, and the story-runner-hardening absorb came through clean (4 `status:`, 4 `slug:`); neither is a tested guarantee, so the post-absorb check is `dt-story validate` on the affected story file. Owner: infrastructure.

- [ ] **`absorb-devloop.sh` cannot resume, and its own hand-off trips the Gate-2 pre-commit hook** (both surfaced 2026-08-17 absorbing the story-runner-hardening story; they compound, so they are filed together). (a) **No resume**: the script has no in-progress detection — no `sequencer`/`CHERRY_PICK_HEAD` check — and `:168` starts a fresh `git cherry-pick`, which git refuses while one is active. Its documented contract (`:32` exit 3, `:171`) is to hand off to plain git on conflict, so re-running after resolving does nothing useful. (b) **The hand-off then blocks**: a clean `git cherry-pick` does not run `pre-commit`, but `git cherry-pick --continue` completes through the normal commit path and does — so the Gate-2 binding refuses every devloop commit in the queue for want of a verdict artifact, which lives in the run dir and does not travel with the patch. Its advice ("run `./scripts/layer-all.sh`") is unfollowable on the host, where layer 7 has no cluster. Net effect: the first conflict in any absorb strands the operator. Fix: run the script's own picks with hooks disabled (`git -c core.hooksPath=/dev/null cherry-pick …`) and say so in the summary — legitimate because the content was validated on the source branch and the hook documents itself as "LOCAL-ONLY / ADVISORY … not a security boundary", with CI's from-scratch re-run as the real enforcement. Add in-progress detection that continues the existing queue instead of starting a new one. Note (a) has a second trigger independent of conflicts: `git cherry` compares patch-ids, so a planning commit **amended on the target after the clone branched** is not recognised as already-absorbed and is queued as an empty pick the operator must `--skip` — which is exactly how this absorb began. Owner: infrastructure.

- [ ] **Devloops wiring up new code-quality tooling don't auto-fix the existing surface** (surfaced 2026-06-24 during task #28's Gate 2): when a devloop introduces a new lint/format/type-check rule that applies to an existing language surface, the rule starts producing violations on code that was authored before the rule existed. The devloop introducing the rule typically ships green (its own code conforms; the rule has nothing to compare against in-diff). But every subsequent devloop touching the same surface inherits the violations as "pre-existing branch debt" and blocks at Gate 2/3 — surfacing as "I want to do my work but X unrelated files violate a rule I didn't introduce." Two concrete cases on this branch: (1) task #17 wired up Prettier + ESLint config over `packages/sdk-core/`, but #11's TS code (authored before #17 was wired) never saw prettier; the formatting violations surfaced first during #12's planning and then again during #28's Gate 2, with both implementers stalled on cross-boundary cleanup that isn't their lane. (2) Same shape would apply to a future devloop wiring up a new clippy lint, a new dt-guard check, or a stricter tsc flag — the rule lands clean against an empty diff, then bites every subsequent devloop on the same surface. Whatever the fix shape is (rule-introducing-devloop runs auto-fix as part of its scope / Lead-side checklist when reviewing tooling-introducing plans / a separate "branch-health" devloop variant that lands the auto-fix sweep alongside the rule / something else), the principle is: a devloop introducing a rule should leave the existing surface compliant with the rule by the time it commits, so subsequent devloops never inherit "pre-existing rule violations" as a Gate-2 blocker. Solution open — needs scoping. Owner: operations (devloop workflow design) + infrastructure (any tooling support).

- [x] **`validate-env-config` silently skips MC + MH (per-instance deployment filenames) — false-confidence STATUS=OK** (surfaced 2026-07-06 by @operations at task #6 Gate-3 review; accepted spin-out, @team-lead-endorsed). `dt-guard env-config`'s workload discovery `find_workload()` (`crates/dt-guard/src/env_config.rs:53-58`) only recognizes the literal filenames `deployment.yaml` / `statefulset.yaml`. AC (`statefulset.yaml`) and GC (`deployment.yaml`) match and are validated; **MC and MH use per-instance names** (`mc-0-deployment.yaml` / `mc-1-deployment.yaml`, `mh-0-deployment.yaml` / `mh-1-deployment.yaml`) so `find_workload` returns `None` → the guard emits `WARN dt-guard auxiliary skip (no workload manifest)` and moves on, yet still exits `STATUS=OK REASON=env-config-clean-4-services`. Net effect: the config↔deployment cross-check (Checks 1-3: required env vars present in workload; `configMapKeyRef` keys exist in configmap; configmap keys referenced by ≥1 workload) provides **zero coverage for two of four services**, and the `-4-services` REASON overcounts (only AC+GC were actually validated). This is the same false-confidence / silent-skip class task #50 addressed — a green guard that isn't checking what the reader assumes. Concretely bit task #6: the 4 OTel keys had to be surfaced in BOTH `mc-0` and `mc-1` deployments (the "easy to half-do" case), and that invariant shipped correct ONLY because @operations hand-verified it — the guard could not. **Fix (three parts):** (a) `find_workload` must discover multiple per-instance workloads — glob `*-deployment.yaml` / `*-statefulset.yaml` in the service dir (falling back to the canonical singular names), returning a set rather than an `Option`; (b) decide **union-vs-intersection semantics** across the discovered instance workloads — a key present in `mc-0` but missing in `mc-1` is precisely the drift to catch, so Checks 1 & 3 want **all-instances (intersection of presence)** not any-instance, while Check 2 (`configMapKeyRef` → configmap key exists) is per-workload; (c) covers **MH identically** (same per-instance topology). Add multi-workload test fixtures (a service dir with two `-N-deployment.yaml` files, one missing a key → must FAIL). Consider hardening the no-workload skip to a hard FAIL (not WARN) when the dir contains `*-deployment.yaml`/`*-statefulset.yaml` but no recognized workload, so a future naming scheme can't silently reopen the hole. Non-trivial (>10 LoC + design decision on semantics + new test surface + touches two services) → correctly outside task #6's changeset. Cross-ref: §Polyglot Pipeline Follow-ups (dt-guard / ADR-0034 guard pipeline is the same binary). **Schedule as a focused infrastructure dt-guard devloop.** Owner: infrastructure (dt-guard maintainer). Provenance: `docs/devloop-outputs/2026-07-05-mc-otel-wiring-task6/main.md`. **RESOLVED 2026-08-28** in `docs/devloop-outputs/2026-08-28-env-config-guard-per-instance-workloads/main.md`. **Semantics that actually landed** (this entry posed the union-vs-intersection question, so recording the answer is the point — the next person to touch this guard will look here first): **Check 1 (required env vars) — PER-WORKLOAD.** Every discovered workload must independently declare every `MissingEnvVar` from `config.rs`. This is the entry's "intersection of presence": a var in `mc-0` but not `mc-1` is a real defect (that pod CrashLoops at half capacity while its sibling stays healthy) and is now caught. **Check 2 (`configMapKeyRef` resolves) — NAME-SCOPED, per workload.** The `(configMapKeyRef.name, key)` PAIR is resolved against that specific ConfigMap's `data:` block, never a directory-wide union of every key in sight. A union would have been strictly WEAKER than the guard it replaced: it would newly pass `mh-0-deployment.yaml` naming `mh-service-config` for a key that only `mh-0-config` declares — a manifest kubelet refuses to start the pod on. An unresolvable ConfigMap name is its own rule id, `configmap_not_found`. **Check 3 (orphan keys) — NAME-SCOPED UNION.** A key is an orphan iff NO workload references *(that ConfigMap's name, that key)*. Union across workloads (so `mh-0-config`'s key, referenced only by `mh-0-deployment.yaml`, is correctly not an orphan) but scoped by ConfigMap name (so a key added to the wrong instance's ConfigMap is still caught, which a name-blind union hides because *a* workload references *that key name*). **Discovery — by parsed `kind:`, NOT the `*-deployment.yaml` glob this entry proposed.** A glob replaces one literal with a longer one and reopens the hole at the next naming change, and it would have minted a third mirror of the per-instance ordinal convention already encoded in `infra/kind/scripts/setup.sh` and the service `kustomization.yaml`s. A manifest kind classified as neither pod-carrying nor pod-spec-free is now a hard FAIL, so a future naming or kind change cannot silently reopen the hole. **The no-workload skip is a hard FAIL**, as this entry suggested considering, along with four sibling silent-skip paths found in the same function (missing `config.rs`/infra dir, `envFrom`, unparseable manifest, workload without a pod spec). `checked_services` now counts only services actually checked, and the OK line reports `env-config-clean-<S>-services-<W>-workloads` so a dropped instance manifest is visible in the status line itself. Remediated the four orphan keys this surfaced in `mh-service-config` (see §Observability Debt).
- [ ] **`dt-guard env-config` does not cover `infra/kubernetes/overlays/**` — a declared coverage boundary, not an oversight (surfaced 2026-08-28 by @security at Gate-1 review of the env-config per-instance-workload devloop)**: the guard resolves ConfigMap keys and `configMapKeyRef`s within `infra/services/<svc>/` only. Kind overlays carry live `data:` keys the guard never sees — `infra/kubernetes/overlays/kind/services/{ac,gc,mc}-service/configmap-otel-patch.yaml`, wired via each overlay's `patches:` stanza. Because a Kustomize strategic merge on a ConfigMap is **additive**, an overlay can introduce a key that no base ConfigMap declares and no workload references, and it is invisible to Checks 2 and 3 — in the surface most likely to be edited during an incident. Verified at the same review: no overlay today creates a ConfigMap that a base workload references, and there is no `configMapGenerator` anywhere in the tree (all eight service kustomizations checked), so there is no live defect — this is a scope gap, not a bug. **Why it is not folded into the guard now**: overlays need *patch* semantics (a partial document merged onto a named base resource) rather than the *declaration* semantics the guard implements; that is a different resolution model plus a kustomize-build dependency, and it is task-sized. **Why it is tracked rather than left implicit**: after the 2026-08-28 fix the guard emits `env-config-clean-<S>-services-<W>-workloads`, which a reader will reasonably take to mean "this service's ConfigMap surface is checked." Shipping that line over an unaudited surface would reproduce, one directory up, the exact false-confidence defect the fix removed. The boundary is also stated in the `crates/dt-guard/src/env_config.rs` module doc so it is visible at the code, not only here. **Action**: extend `env-config` (or add a sibling policy) to resolve overlay ConfigMap patches against their base, so an overlay-introduced key is either referenced or reported. **Related design note**: if a workload ever needs to reference a ConfigMap supplied from OUTSIDE the service directory, the agreed shape is an **explicit declared list of externally-supplied ConfigMap names** (visible, reviewable, config-over-hardcoding) — NOT an implicit union fallback that resolves a name it cannot see against keys it can, which was considered and rejected at Gate 1 as empty-collection-means-clean in a different hat. Owner: infrastructure (dt-guard maintainer). Provenance: `docs/devloop-outputs/2026-08-28-env-config-guard-per-instance-workloads/main.md`.
- [ ] **dt-guard wrappers exec `target/release/dt-guard` gated only on existence, never freshness — a stale binary can produce a green verdict against unbuilt code (surfaced 2026-08-28 by @security + @operations at review of the env-config per-instance-workload devloop)**: `scripts/guards/simple/_dt_guard_wrapper.sh` resolves `DT_GUARD=${DT_GUARD:-$REPO_ROOT/target/release/dt-guard}` and gates solely on `[[ -x "$DT_GUARD" ]]` — it never checks the binary is newer than `crates/dt-guard/src/`. The full pipeline is safe: `scripts/lang/rust/compile.sh` builds `target/release/dt-guard` and `for_each_lang_with_verb` is always-run with no skip-if-untouched, so `layer-all.sh` cannot run a stale binary. But **two entry points reach the guards without compiling first**: (a) standalone `scripts/layer3.sh`, documented as a legitimate entry point at `scripts/layer-all.sh` (the layer scripts are individually runnable); and (b) the `scripts/guards/run-guards.sh` invocation the devloop skill directs the Lead to make at Gate 1 and Gate 2 (`.claude/skills/devloop/SKILL.md`). This is not hypothetical — it is exactly how this task's first wrapper run reported `STATUS=OK REASON=env-config-clean-4-services` (the OLD token) from a binary that predated the fix: `cargo run`/`cargo build` had refreshed only the *debug* profile while the wrapper ran the stale *release* artifact. A green guard verdict over code that does not contain the guard is this task's own defect (a control reporting OK over surface it did not actually evaluate) reproduced one layer up, in the pipeline rather than the policy. **Why the obvious fix is unsafe**: an mtime comparison of the binary against `crates/dt-guard/src/` false-fails whenever cargo declines to relink because nothing changed — the normal state on a warm `target/` with a fresh checkout — converting a real green run into a spurious red. **Fix shape**: a build-stamp carrying the source-tree hash, written by `compile.sh` at build time and checked by `_dt_guard_wrapper.sh` before exec; mismatch → `STATUS=PRECONDITION_FAILURE REASON=dt-guard-binary-stale` (operator lane, not a violation). Cross-cutting: 8 wrappers share the prelude, plus the rust compile verb, plus a design call on the stamp format — genuinely task-sized, which is why the *fix* is deferred; the *tracking* is not. Owner: infrastructure (dt-guard maintainer) + operations. Provenance: `docs/devloop-outputs/2026-08-28-env-config-guard-per-instance-workloads/main.md`.

- [x] **CLOSED 2026-08-15 — `grep`: flags placed after a `--` end-of-options terminator are parsed as operands** (surfaced 2026-08-15 during story task #3 / R-7; **entry substantially corrected on the same day — see below**). The durable one-liner: **when you pass `--` to grep, every later argument is an operand — put option flags before the `--`, and reserve `--` for when the pattern may itself begin with `-`.** Measured on a synthetic tree with `/usr/bin/grep`:

  ```
  grep -rn -F     NEEDLE /tmp/pt --exclude-dir=docs   -> exclusion honored,  rc 0
  grep -rn -F --  NEEDLE /tmp/pt --exclude-dir=docs   -> exclusion IGNORED,  rc 2
  grep -rn --exclude-dir=docs -F -- NEEDLE /tmp/pt    -> exclusion honored,  rc 0
  ```

  **Sweep DONE, result: zero other sites. This is closed, not open.** Every `--exclude*`/`--include*` on a `grep` invocation in the repo was the one in `scripts/guards/simple/validate-subdomain-regex-sync.sh`, fixed in that same commit. The only other `--exclude` hits are `git ls-files --exclude-standard`, which is a git flag and unrelated.

  **PREMISE CORRECTED 2026-08-15 (@operations), same day, before anyone acted on it.** This entry originally claimed: (1) "`grep` in the devloop container is `ugrep` 7.5.0"; (2) "ugrep does NOT permute options after operands", unlike GNU grep; (3) the failure is silent "with no warning and exit status unchanged"; (4) the blast radius is "every post-operand `--exclude*`/`--include*` in the repo", marked **NOT SWEPT** with an instruction to treat prior clean checks as unverified, owned by `infrastructure`. **All four were wrong**, and the root cause of the error is worth more than the finding was:

  - `/usr/bin/grep` is **GNU grep 3.8**, and that is what every guard, every layer script and CI actually execute. `grep --version` reports ugrep **only inside a Claude Code agent's own Bash-tool shell**, where the harness defines `grep` as a shell *function* (`type grep` shows it) that shims the `claude` binary. That function is not exported and does not exist under `bash script.sh`. The original measurement was taken in the agent shell and attributed to the container.
  - **Both greps permute options after operands identically.** The real mechanism is the `--` terminator, which happened to be present in the reproduction command.
  - It is **not silent**: both emit `grep: --exclude-dir=docs: No such file or directory` and exit **2**.
  - The sweep is one command; its answer is complete; ownership was never `infrastructure`'s (it is shell idiom in the validation pipeline) and there is nothing left to own.

  Corrected in place rather than deleted, per this story's own precedent for corrected premises: the original text asserted a **fail-open defect in validation tooling** with an owner and an explicit "prior clean checks are unverified" instruction, so deleting it would leave the claim citable while removing the correction. **Generalisable lesson, and the reason this is kept: a measurement of the *environment* taken from inside an agent's tool shell is not a measurement of the environment scripts run in.** Verify with `bash -c` or a script file, not the interactive tool shell. Provenance: `docs/devloop-outputs/2026-08-15-layer7-per-run-org/main.md` §Issues Encountered #2.

- [ ] **`layer7.sh`'s cluster-teardown path has no busy-tolerance while its setup path does — a benign helper collision reports as `cluster-rebuild-failed`** (surfaced 2026-08-15 during story R-7 task #3 Gate 2; deferred by Lead ruling with justification, not silently). **(a) The asymmetry**: `__dev_cluster_setup()` in `scripts/layer7.sh` IS busy-tolerant — it captures the client's output, greps it for `(busy)` / `in-flight write` / `another write`, calls `__poll_setup_idle` and retries once. The `"$DEV_CLUSTER" teardown` call in the `infra/kind/` rebuild branch of the same file is **bare**: `|| precondition_fail cluster-rebuild-failed`, with no busy detection and no retry. The retry helper already exists, in the same file, a few dozen lines away. **(b) The consequence**: a collision that the helper's write mutex handled correctly becomes `PRECONDITION_FAILURE / cluster-rebuild-failed`, whose runbook row tells the operator "the cluster may be in a partially-torn-down state" and sends them to `/tmp/devloop/helper.log`. The cluster is fine; the other writer simply got there first. That is R-4's misattribution class — an environment condition reported as a specific fault requiring inspection — inside the pipeline built to prevent it. **(c) Reachability is MEASURED, not theoretical** (so the next person need not re-derive it): `/tmp/devloop/helper.log` recorded `{"cmd":"rejected_busy","args":["rejected=teardown","in_flight=teardown"],"exit_code":-1,"outcome":"rejected"}` — two `teardown` verbs **500ms apart**, from two `layer-all.sh` runs against one helper. Every line in that run's `layer-7.stderr.log` was duplicated, which is the fingerprint to look for. Layer 7 died at 3 seconds, in Phase 1e, so Phase 1h never ran. Trigger condition: **two devloops sharing one helper**, which is the normal state of a container running an Agent-Teams loop. **(d) Premise correction, recorded per this story's convention**: the Gate-1 ruling that stood down busy-tolerance work said *"with no socket call there is no write slot to contend, so generalizing `__dev_cluster_setup` would churn working code for nothing."* That is true of **Phase 1h**, which makes no socket call, and **false of the teardown path**, which makes one and was observed contending. The ruling's conclusion still holds for task #3 (the teardown line is byte-identical to its pre-task version, so this is new work on a pre-existing path, not "fix, don't defer" on the task's own diff); its reasoning does not extend here. Corrected in place so the original sentence is not later citable as evidence that the whole class was assessed and dismissed. **Fix shape**: reuse the existing busy-detect + `__poll_setup_idle` + retry-once logic for the teardown call — either by extracting the shared shape or by calling it directly. Behaviour change to the operator-lane boundary, so it wants @operations' design input rather than a drive-by. **(e) Owner: operations.** Provenance: `docs/devloop-outputs/2026-08-15-layer7-per-run-org/main.md` §Accepted Deferrals.

- [ ] **The repo's only `bash -n` sweep is wired into nothing — it runs only when invoked by hand** (surfaced 2026-08-15 during story R-7 task #3). `scripts/lang/_get_base_ref.behavior-equivalence.test.sh` case 7a syntax-checks every `*.sh` under `scripts/` and `infra/` — **117 files** after task #3 widened it from `guards/simple` + `common.sh` (~30). It is the guard for the exact defect class that task #3 hit: a stray `fi` made `scripts/layer7.sh` entirely unparseable, and an unparseable layer script exits from the shell itself with **no STATUS line, no REASON and no lane**, so `layer-all` records `UNKNOWN`. That defect was caught incidentally, by a self-test that happens to execute the script, rather than by design. **The problem**: grepping `scripts/`, `.github/` and the whole repo finds **zero** references to this test file outside itself. It is not in `layer3.sh`'s `run_and_emit` list, not in any workflow, not in `run-guards.sh`'s discovery glob (it is not under `guards/simple/`). So the sweep exists and does not run. **Why it was not simply wired in**: the file currently has **2 pre-existing failures** (`ci-push-guardrail-skip` and one other), verified independently — by @test and by task #3's implementer — to be identical with and without task #3's edit. Wiring it into Layer 3 as-is would red the gate on unrelated debt, which trains people to ignore Layer 3 — "fail loudly, never mask" violated in the other direction. **Fix shape**: fix or quarantine the 2 failing cases, then add one `run_and_emit` line to `scripts/layer3.sh`. Consider whether the 7a sweep deserves to be its own always-run check rather than a case inside a base-ref equivalence test, since its subject matter is unrelated to that file's stated purpose and its value is much broader. Owner: operations. Provenance: `docs/devloop-outputs/2026-08-15-layer7-per-run-org/main.md` §Accepted Deferrals.

## Infrastructure Validation — `validate-kustomize` fail-opens when kustomize/kubeconform are absent

- [ ] **`dt-guard validate-kustomize` maps "I did not check this" onto the same exit code as "I checked and it was clean", and the CI runner almost certainly hits the uncovered path on every run (owner: `operations` for the fail-open flip + emit_ok sweep, `infrastructure` for the image/CI tool install; found 2026-09-02 at Gate 2 of `docs/devloop-outputs/2026-09-02-frame-v2-cross-language-vectors/`, surfaced by @operations because the OPS-8 exit-0 WARN fix in that devloop finally made the skip visible, mechanism confirmed by @test)**: `crates/dt-guard/src/kustomize.rs:255-290` has two degradation levels. kubeconform absent → R-17 schema validation skipped; **kustomize/kubectl absent → R-15/R-17/R-18/R-19 ALL skipped** (`:263-271`). Both `warn_skip(...)` to **stderr** (`common/scan.rs:22`) and then `emit_ok("kustomize-tool-absent-skipped" | "kustomize-clean-kubeconform-skipped")` to **stdout** (`common/status.rs:14`), exiting 0.

  **The fail-open is at the exit code, not the token.** Under Layer 3 the chain is: dt-guard exits 0 → `run-guards.sh` non-verbose captures `$OUTPUT` (`:217`) and, on the pass arm, discards everything except the new `^WARN ` grep → `layer3.sh`'s `run_and_emit` emits `STATUS=OK REASON=guards-passed`. So dt-guard's own `STATUS=OK REASON=...-skipped` **never reaches `tee_collect_statuses`**, and the stderr WARN is advisory. `emit_ok` sits on the code path that precedes `exit 0`, so the ONLY thing distinguishing "not checked" from "checked, clean" is a reason token nothing in the run-guards path reads. This framing survives someone later noticing the STATUS line is discarded — the finding is the exit-code equivalence, not a misleading gate token.

  **Almost certainly live in CI, and always has been.** `.github/workflows/ci.yml` installs only `protobuf-compiler` (`:42-43`, `:149-150`) and runs `./scripts/layer-all.sh` (`:118`); there is no kustomize, kubectl, or kubeconform step. If `detect_tool()` returns `None` on `ubuntu-latest`, R-15/R-17/R-18/R-19 have reported OK without executing on every run since the guard landed. **Confirm empirically** (assert the tools resolve in CI) rather than trusting the runner image.

  **Fix, in this order — order is the whole answer.** (1) Install and SHA-pin `kubeconform` + `kustomize` in the devloop image and add a CI step (the Dockerfile pattern already exists at `infra/devloop/Dockerfile:46`,`:76` — `echo "${SHA}  /usr/local/bin/<tool>" | sha256sum -c -`). (2) THEN flip tool-absence from skip-and-pass to fail-closed. Flipping first reds every environment lacking the tools until (1) lands, which makes *deleting the guard* the cheapest route to green — the exact g14 anti-pattern rejected in this devloop. (3) Sweep for sibling `emit_ok(*-skipped)` idioms: a reason token that says "I did not check this" mapped onto the OK enum reads as coverage from every consumer that gates on the enum. Steps 1 alone leaves the fail-open mechanism in place for the next missing tool.

  **Adjacent latent hazard, worth a self-test guard, not live today:** under `run-guards.sh --verbose` the guard is not captured (`:211`) and streams live, so under `layer3.sh` dt-guard's own `^STATUS=` lines flow into `tee_collect_statuses` as layer votes. Benign now (it only emits `OK`/`FAIL`, both valid enums, and `layer3.sh` never passes `--verbose`) but it is the OPS-3 coupling — a guard emitting `STATUS=` couples it to the collector — so name it before someone adds `--verbose` for debugging and silently changes aggregation semantics. Pre-existing, correctly out of task 8's scope.

## Developer Experience

Rationale: two described modes with override rules is exactly the mirrored-prose drift risk the repo's SSoT convention warns about; after the runner is the normal execution path, interactive prose is dead weight that a Lead can still wander into. Interactive use remains possible (a human can always run `/devloop` in a session and react to the escalation file themselves) — it just stops being a separately documented protocol. Do NOT do this before the experiment concludes; the current two-mode state is deliberate during transition. Owner: operations. Surfaced 2026-08-01 while drafting the run-story deliverables.
