- [ ] **Python in the guard pipeline — language strategy + toolchain plumbing (debate-worthy)**. Surfaced 2026-05-14 during task #39-followup (`docs/devloop-outputs/2026-05-14-doc-citation-durability-guards/`) Gate-3 close-out when the user asked whether the new `.py` module was a fresh dependency. Audit found six pre-existing simple guards already use inline Python heredocs (`validate-alert-rules.sh`, `validate-infrastructure-metrics.sh`, `validate-dashboard-panels.sh`, `validate-application-metrics.sh`, `validate-metric-labels.sh`, `grafana-datasources.sh`) — multi-month convention, never formalized. Task #39-followup added the first **committed `.py` module** at `scripts/guards/lib/doc_cite_extract.py`, consumed via `sys.path.insert(0, "<repo_root>/scripts/guards/lib")` by three guards. Current gaps: no `requirements.txt` / `pyproject.toml` / version manifest anywhere; no Python interpreter version pin (devloop image relies on Debian-bookworm's system `python3` = 3.11, would drift silently on image bumps); no Python lint or type-check guard (Rust has clippy, TS has eslint, proto has buf lint — Python has nothing); no documented import convention; `__pycache__/` `.gitignore` entry added without a rationale comment. Three plausible end states for the debate to converge on: **(A) Standardize on Python** — formal `scripts/guards/lib/` package + `requirements.txt` + Python lint guard (e.g. ruff) + version pin in a shared shell helper; rewrite simple bash guards where Python would be cleaner. **(B) Standardize on bash** — rewrite the 6 existing heredoc guards in pure bash (or jq/yq for structured data); abandon the committed `.py` module + revert task #39-followup's Python module to bash. **(C) Formalized polyglot** — keep both with a written contract for choosing each (e.g., "structured data parsing → Python; pattern matching → bash") and add the missing Python toolchain plumbing. Suggested `/debate "Python in the guard pipeline — formalize, consolidate, or back away?"` with participants infrastructure (devloop image + scripts/) + operations (guards + runbooks) + security (Python ReDoS / supply chain) + test (guard validation surface) + code-reviewer (style + consistency + ADR compliance) + dry-reviewer (cross-guard duplication patterns). Likely produces an ADR. Out of scope: rewriting individual guard logic; this is about language strategy + toolchain plumbing only. Owner: operations (debate convener); resolution likely ADR-track.

- [ ] **Layer-table row duplicated between `SKILL.md` and ADR-0033 has now intentionally diverged, with nothing recording why** (surfaced 2026-07-29 by @test at task #20 Gate 2). The Always-Run/Skip-If-Untouched Layer 7 row exists verbatim in two places: `.claude/skills/devloop/SKILL.md` (§Always-Run vs Skip-If-Untouched matrix) and `docs/decisions/adr-0033-polyglot-validation-pipeline.md` (§3 canonical layer table). Task #20 marked the SKILL.md copy "Playwright @smoke: pending #18/#19" and left the ADR copy reading "+ Playwright @smoke". **That divergence is correct, not a bug** — the two documents have different genres: SKILL.md is an operational instruction read present-tense by every devloop, so an unbuilt tier must be marked; the ADR is a design record of what was decided, and adding status markers to ADRs runs directly against the tracked decision in §Documentation Hygiene ("Remove status/tracking content from all ADRs — ADRs are now design records only"). The problem is that **the justification is written down nowhere**, so a future reader diffing the two rows sees a mismatch and may "correct" it in either direction — re-introducing the present-tense claim into SKILL.md, or pushing status content into the ADR. Fix options: (a) one inline note on the SKILL.md row stating it deliberately carries build-status the ADR does not, and why; (b) have the SKILL.md row cite the ADR as the design target rather than restating its text, so there is one copy. (b) is the CLAUDE.md single-source-of-truth answer and is the smaller surface. **Do NOT implement the guard shape originally proposed for this** (asserting the SKILL.md row against `scripts/layer7.sh`'s actual command): @test proposed it at Gate 1 and then withdrew it — such a guard would flag every legitimate forward reference as drift, which is exactly the pattern ADR-0033 §3 and the #56 Meta-note say to *mark pending*, not delete. A guard here would have to compare the two doc rows to each other, not either row to the script. Natural pickup is story task #19, which already opens `SKILL.md` `--paired-with=operations`. Owner: test (SKILL.md Layer-7 text) + operations (SKILL.md file). Provenance: task #20 Gate-1 row-7 exchange, @team-lead ruling 2026-07-29.

- [ ] **`BUDGET_BREACH` is one global 20s threshold applied to every layer, so Layers 3 and 4 breach on EVERY run and the token trains operators to ignore it — while the same file already records that exact argument as the reason Layer 7 is excluded (owner: operations; trigger: the next change to `scripts/layer-all.sh` cost signalling, or the next time a real cost regression needs to be visible)**: confirmed 2026-09-05 at Gate 2 of `docs/devloop-outputs/2026-09-05-sdk-frame-v2-sframe-stack/` as **pre-existing, not introduced** — the reviewed run emitted `WARN BUDGET_BREACH LAYER=3 DURATION=47` and `LAYER=4 DURATION=180` against `BUDGET=20`, and Layer 3 at 47s is *below* the ~50.5s baseline recorded in `docs/runbooks/devloop-validation.md` §6.3, so nothing in that diff moved it. `scripts/layer-all.sh:107` sets `budget_secs_per_layer="${DEVLOOP_LAYER_BUDGET_SECS:-20}"` for all layers except 7. **The contradiction is in the same file**: the exclusion comment at `scripts/layer-all.sh:170-173` justifies skipping Layer 7 because "a Layer-7 `BUDGET_BREACH` would false-fire every run and train operators to ignore the token" — which is a correct piece of alert-fatigue reasoning that is then applied to one of the three layers that need it. A warning that has fired on every run for months is not a warning; it is noise that will also be ignored on the run where Layer 3 genuinely regresses, which is the only run it exists for. **Shape if built**: per-layer budgets seeded from the baselines already recorded in the runbook (Layer 3 ~50.5s; the 90s p95 for the 3+6 fast tier is already a separate, correctly-scoped `BUDGET_TOTAL_BREACH`), rather than one constant that is wrong for two layers by construction. **Deliberately not fixed in the devloop that confirmed it**: choosing the per-layer numbers is a decision with the runbook's recorded baselines as its input, not a threshold edit, and it changes the cost-signalling surface for every devloop from inside an unrelated client task.

- [ ] **Layer 4 reports a linker abort under memory pressure as `cargo-test-failed`, which names the diff as the culprit and sends triage at the tests (owner: `infrastructure` for the wrapper machinery, `test` as affected consumer; filed 2026-09-08 by @operations at Gate 3 of `docs/devloop-outputs/2026-09-08-mc-steer-client-to-edge-handler/`; trigger: the next touch of `scripts/lang/rust/test.sh` or `layer5.sh`, or the next occurrence)**: observed at Gate 2 attempt 1 of that devloop — `collect2: fatal error: ld terminated with signal 6 [Aborted], core dumped`, **thirteen** `mc-service` integration test binaries failing to **link** on a 16 GB machine with ~1 GB free, several of them (`gc_integration`, `heartbeat_tasks`, `token_refresh_integration`, `redis_metrics_integration`) untouched by the diff under review. It did not reproduce on an isolated `layer4.sh` re-run. **The defect is the classification, not the OOM**: `lang/rust/test.sh` emits `REASON=cargo-test-failed` for any non-zero `cargo test`, and `docs/runbooks/devloop-validation.md` §6.4's row for that token said, in terms, "fix the test". A machine-resource failure therefore arrives wearing a **confident instruction to investigate the wrong thing** — worse than an ambiguous signal, because the reader acts on it. It cost that devloop a full pipeline cycle and an hour of the implementer hunting their own diff. **This is the same rule the review protocol applies to test assertions, one level up**: a probe failure and a content failure must not share a reason token, because the one that gets triaged as the other is then "fixed" by relaxing the wrong thing. **Shape if built**: detect `signal 6` / `signal 9` attributed to `collect2`/`ld`/`rust-lld` in the wrapper's captured output and emit an environment/precondition classification into the operator lane rather than `cargo-test-failed` — the vocabulary already exists (`PRECONDITION_FAILURE:`, ADR-0035's operator lane, `record_infra_incident()`), and `scripts/guards/run-guards.sh:classify_guard_exit` is the precedent for exit-triage shape. **Why it is task-sized rather than a one-line grep, and this is the part that needs the budget**: a *genuine* link error — undefined symbol, duplicate symbol, a missing native lib — **IS** the diff's fault and must keep reaching the implementer lane. Getting the discriminator wrong in the permissive direction creates a hole that silently routes real breakage to the operator, which is strictly worse than today's noise. Layer 5 drives the same linker and needs the same treatment; do not fix one and leave the other. **Interim control**: `docs/runbooks/devloop-validation.md` §6.4 now carries a dedicated row (symptom, the multiple-unrelated-binaries tell, and check-memory-then-re-run-in-isolation as first action) with a matching §8 catalogue entry, landed by @operations in the devloop that hit it. That row is the only thing separating the two failures until this lands — **delete it when this entry closes**, not before.

- [ ] **A `layer-all.sh` verdict is an assertion about a tree state, and nothing binds it to the tree it was computed over — so a run contaminated mid-flight impersonates a test failure (owner: `infrastructure` for the `layer-all.sh` machinery, `test` as affected consumer; filed 2026-09-08 by @operations at Gate 3 of `docs/devloop-outputs/2026-09-08-mc-steer-client-to-edge-handler/`, from an observation the implementer recorded rather than claimed; trigger: the next touch of `scripts/layer-all.sh`)**: the implementer of that devloop twice invalidated their own pipeline run by editing under it, and detected it only via an **ad-hoc `git status` wrapper around one invocation** — explicitly *not* a property of `layer-all.sh`, which is why it was recorded as a gap rather than as a fix that landed. Today a mid-run edit surfaces as whatever layer happens to trip, most often a test failure, so it arrives labelled as the diff's fault. **Same misattribution class as the linker-abort entry above, different mechanism**, and the same remedy shape: a contaminated run and a genuine failure have different owners and different remedies, so they must not share a token. **Shape if built**: capture `git status --porcelain` plus `HEAD` at entry, re-check at exit, and on divergence emit a **distinct STATUS token** naming tree contamination — never fold it into `FAIL`. **Two cautions, both load-bearing.** (a) **No `--allow-dirty` escape hatch.** A bypass flag becomes the default the first time someone is in a hurry, and the control is then gone while still appearing to exist — this tree has already barred that pattern elsewhere. (b) **The check must not watch paths the pipeline itself writes.** A control that cries wolf gets disabled, and a disabled control is worse than none because the disabling is invisible later; enumerate what the layers write before choosing the watch set, rather than assuming build output is all gitignored. Provenance for the token-separation argument: that devloop spent its entire review budget establishing it for the R-15 env-test gate (four distinct reason tokens, each naming its lane) — the reasoning transfers unchanged and does not need re-deriving here.

## Process / Review-Protocol

### A review verdict has no as-of commit, so post-verdict edits fall silently inside its scope (2026-09-09, story task #22)

**Owner**: process. Surfaced by @dry-reviewer at Gate 2 of task #22 and confirmed live: a
reviewer issued a clean verdict on `client-media.json`, three edits then landed on that
file, and the verdict silently covered a state it never saw — one of the new edits
introduced a fresh finding (F-3, a restated count) that the ACK now appeared to bless. The
finding was caught only because the implementer *disclosed* the post-verdict edits, which
prompted a re-read; nothing structural pins a verdict to the artifact state it was issued
against. **Candidate remedy**: a verdict names the commit SHA it was issued against, so a
later edit to a reviewed file is visibly outside the ACK's scope rather than inside it by
default. Task-sized (touches the review-protocol contract and the devloop record schema);
out of scope for task #22. This is the reviewer-side form of the same read-the-artifact
class the task's `dt_client_*` inspection obligation addresses on the author side.



- [ ] **Amend `.claude/skills/devloop/review-protocol.md` §Assertion Vacuity mechanism 4 (owner: test, operations co-sign; filed 2026-09-08 from `docs/devloop-outputs/2026-09-05-sender-id-binding-contract/`)**. **Form agreed by both co-owners: amend mechanism 4, do NOT carve a sixth mechanism.** The finding: an expectation **correctly derived from the artifact** (satisfying 4's provenance clause) can still be vacuous when the derived value coincides with the value a degenerate implementation would return — an allocator that issues `1` to the first joiner makes the honestly-derived expectation identical to a hardcoded `1`. This is not a new mechanism; it is the **proof that mechanism 4's second clause is non-optional**. 4's remedy already reads "derive it from the artifact AND run it against a real adverse input before believing it"; the protocol worked when followed literally, and what failed was @security's S2 paraphrase, which kept the derivation clause and dropped the adverse-input one. A sixth mechanism would only add a sixth thing to paraphrase-and-drop. **The amendment** lands in 4 as: *derivation establishes provenance, not discrimination; a correctly-derived expectation can coincide with the degenerate value a defect would produce — re-sourcing does not fix this (it is about position, not provenance), only running the mutation the assertion exists to catch and watching it go RED does.* State the run in **falsification form** (mutation shown red, not "exercise an adverse case"), plus an optional head-of-section framing sentence for the broader class — *a control that cannot report on the thing it would be consulted about, and reports clean instead* — which also reaches @operations' OPS-3b (a production instrument recorded before the interval it would measure) and OPS-4 (an alert routed off the signal it exists to catch), neither of which a §Assertion-Vacuity *test* item could carry. **Instance, mutation-verified**: an arm in `crates/mc-service/tests/media_coordination_integration.rs` satisfied @security's derive-from-the-allocator rule and **still passed a hardcoded-`1` mutation**; fixed by joining a decoy first so the id under test is `> 1`. Full provenance in that devloop's `main.md` §Lessons Learned 1. **Lands as its own test-owned change with an operations co-sign trailer, NOT in this devloop's diff** (`review-protocol.md` is co-owned and unrelated to the sender_id wire contract; folding it in would smuggle a co-owned protocol edit past its co-owner).

- [ ] **Add a RELAY-failure mechanism to `.claude/skills/devloop/review-protocol.md` §Assertion Vacuity: a composite claim whose cheap limb is verified launders its expensive limb** (filed 2026-09-09 by @operations from `docs/devloop-outputs/2026-09-09-web-app-in-meeting-loopback/`; owner **operations** for the review-protocol edit, co-signed by @infrastructure who supplied half the mechanism). **This is genuinely a sixth mechanism, not a paraphrase of the five** — and the entry above is the reason to be careful about that claim, since its own conclusion was "amend mechanism 4, do NOT carve a sixth". The five listed mechanisms are all about **an assertion that runs and observes nothing**. This one is about **a claim that travels between reviewers**: nothing is asserted, no test is involved, and the artifact is a message rather than a control. It cannot be folded into 1-5 without stretching "assertion" past the point where the remedies still apply.
  **The mechanism.** A finding is often a composite: one limb cheaply falsifiable (a grep, a class hierarchy, a state machine), one limb expensive (what a rendered string *reads as*, five hops from the throw site). The reviewer checks the cheap limb — because it is cheap — and relays the expensive one. The verified limb then **launders** the unverified one: the composite travels with the credibility of its cheapest part, and each subsequent reader sees a finding that was, demonstrably, checked. **The tell is that it looks maximally rigorous at the moment it is most wrong**, which is why review does not catch it. Effort is inverted exactly where it matters: the claim most likely to be false gets the least verification, and then borrows standing from the claim least likely to be false.
  **Worked instance — it fired at least twice in one devloop, once from a reviewer and once from the Lead.** @operations found that `docs/runbooks/client-dev-local.md`'s new secure-context section stated a symptom the code cannot produce, and — in the same message that instructed the implementer to *derive strings from code rather than from review threads* — supplied a claim about the user-visible error string derived from a review thread ("the error is misattributed to browser support; the developer reads it as unsupported WebTransport"). @infrastructure verified the falsifiable half (`SignalingClient` has no fallback; `MeetingSession`'s state machine puts `connecting-mc` strictly before `joined`), relayed the interpretive half intact, and passed it to @implementer as drafting guidance. It was false: `TransportError extends Error` not `SdkError`, so `SignalingClient#toSignalingError()` **replaces** the message and the user sees `SIGNALING: Signaling transport closed` — generic, byte-identical to F1/F8/F9, never naming WebTransport at all. Caught by @security tracing all six hops. Had it landed, the finding would have injected a **second** false symptom into two files in the same edit that removed the first, carrying reviewer authority that makes it *less* likely to be re-checked, not more.
  **The count is the finding, not the anecdote.** **Three reviewers independently produced a corrected symptom for that one sentence and all three were wrong, in three different directions** (@operations: misattributed to browser support; @security's first pass: the error names the cause; @infrastructure: relayed the first). Only *running the path* settled it. One wrong correction reads as an individual slip; three reads as a property of reviewing prose about runtime behaviour without executing it — which is the claim this entry is making, and it is why the instance is worth more than a note.
  **A second, independent instance from the Lead, same shape.** At Gate 2 the Lead diagnosed a counter defect by verifying the cheap limb (`framesAccepted` is 0) and *inferring* the expensive one (therefore the counter is miswired) from a plausible reading of a `firstMediaFrame: 31ms` bus event, without tracing where that measurement is taken. Corrected by @implementer from source. Note the invariant across every instance: **the correction always came from whoever executed, never from whoever read more carefully.** Re-reading does not fix this class, which is precisely why the remedy has to name a run.
  **CAVEAT ON THE REMEDY, and it is not optional — "run it" is necessary but not sufficient.** @implementer's *first* execution also lied: it returned `Unexpected error`, a harness artifact of two `SdkError` copies in the test module graph making `instanceof` false. The true value appeared only through the real module alias. So a run through a harness whose module graph, bundling or environment differs from production is another cheap limb that can launder an expensive conclusion — the same mechanism one level down. State the environment the run happened in alongside the result, and if it is not the production path, say so.
  **Two halves, both needed.** @infrastructure's: *I verified the falsifiable claim and relayed the interpretive one — I inverted the effort exactly where it mattered.* @operations': reviewer authority is the amplifier, explaining why it was not challenged downstream, but it does not explain why it was not checked upstream; the effort inversion does.
  **Remedy, in falsification form** (per the amendment above — state the run, not the intention): *do not relay a claim about observable behaviour unless you have run or traced it; if you pass something on unverified, mark it unverified in the message rather than folding it into your own finding.* **The second clause is the load-bearing one** — the failure was not that the originator was unsure, it is that **the uncertainty did not survive the handoff**. A composite finding should decompose into its verified and unverified limbs at the point of relay, not travel as one claim carrying one credibility.
  **Why file rather than fix inline**: `review-protocol.md` is co-owned and unrelated to this devloop's diff (ADR-0036 client media), so folding it in would smuggle a co-owned protocol edit past its co-owners — the same rule the entry above applies to itself. **Coordinate with that entry**: both edit §Assertion Vacuity, both are operations-involved, and they should land in one pass rather than two so the section is renumbered once. If the reviewer of that change concludes this collapses into mechanism 4 after all, that is an acceptable outcome — but it should be decided against the worked instance above, not on the general preference for fewer mechanisms.

Two of the story's 26 devloop records carry the literal template placeholders (`**Verdict**: CLEAR / RESOLVED-FIXED / RESOLVED-DEFERRED / ESCALATED` and `{count} found, {count} fixed, {count} deferred`) in that section: `docs/devloop-outputs/2026-09-01-release-premise-and-preflight-guards/main.md` and `docs/devloop-outputs/2026-09-09-web-app-in-meeting-loopback/main.md`. They are the only two in the tree besides `docs/devloop-outputs/_template/main.md` itself, so the detection is a two-literal grep with one path exemption. **The two cases are not equally severe and the check should not conflate them**: the web-app record has a real Gate-3 verdict table elsewhere in the file, so the placeholder is a stale duplicate section; the release-premise record has **no reviewer verdict anywhere in the file**, so the Ownership Lens verdict for its Domain-judgment `scripts/dev-web.sh` row was never recorded at all. **Why this is not cosmetic**: ADR-0024 §6.6 step 7 makes the Gate-3 Ownership Lens verdict the mechanism by which a cross-boundary classification is confirmed or upgraded, and `docs/devloop-outputs/**` is the only durable home for it — a template placeholder reads as *reviewed and clean* to every later reader, including the story-close retrospective that consumes these records. **Wrong fix to pre-empt**: do not make the check assert that a verdict word is present, because `CLEAR` appears in the placeholder line itself; key on the placeholder literals and on `{count}`, which cannot occur in a filled record. Related: the as-of-commit entry above is the same class one level up — a verdict whose scope is unpinned, versus a verdict that was never written.

(An `#[expect]` naming a lint that never fires is itself a warning, which is why the check matters; here it comes out clean.) Surfaced 2026-09-01 by code-reviewer at Gate 3 of `docs/devloop-outputs/2026-09-01-internal-contract-reshape/` and routed cross-owner by @team-lead. Trigger: next change touching that file.
- [ ] **`crates/proto-gen/tests/signaling_roundtrip.rs:18` uses `#![allow(clippy::panic, clippy::expect_used, clippy::unwrap_used)]` where ADR-0002 requires `#[expect(...)]` (owner: protocol)**: ADR-0002 states it as a rule twice — `:290` ("When lints must be suppressed, use `#[expect(...)]` instead of `#[allow(...)]`") and the `:334` checklist item — and `clippy.toml:20` models the form with a `reason =`. The rationale is the self-cleaning property: `#[expect]` warns when the suppression becomes dead, `#[allow]` rots silently. Landed 2026-08-31 with the signalling reshape; **not** fixed in the 2026-09-01 `internal.proto` reshape, where the sibling `internal_roundtrip.rs` was written correctly with `#![expect(clippy::expect_used, reason = "…")]` from the start. **Why not fixed together**: the file is not otherwise in that changeset, and the conversion is not a mechanical swap — an `#[expect]` naming a lint that never fires is itself a warning, so each of the three lints must be checked for whether it actually triggers before being carried over (`clippy::panic` in particular: assert macros do not trip it, so it fires only if there is an explicit `panic!`, which that file does have at its oneof-mismatch arms). Doing that verification inside a proto-reshape commit would have widened the diff into a file the reshape does not touch, for a lint-form change. Surfaced 2026-09-01 by code-reviewer at Gate 3 of `docs/devloop-outputs/2026-09-01-internal-contract-reshape/`, who explicitly declined "the sibling does it too" as scope-lock — correctly, since it is a same-owner (protocol) pre-existing deviation, not a licence. Natural moment: the next change to touch that file.

- [ ] **`validate-knowledge-index` reports brace-expansion citations as `stale_pointer`, and its in-scope window is what makes the shape look safe (2026-08-17)**: Surfaced at the `story-runner-hardening` story close, where four of five violations were this one authoring shape across three specialists' INDEXes (@team-lead's count) — including one I introduced myself in `docs/specialist-knowledge/dry-reviewer/INDEX.md` and hand-flattened. Policy lives in `crates/dt-guard/src/knowledge_index.rs`.

  **Mechanism, measured rather than described.** `is_glob_or_placeholder()` at `:96` skips a citation containing `*` or `NNNN`; it says nothing about `{a,b}`, so a brace group falls through to the literal `abs.exists()` test at `:165` and reds even when every expansion exists. Two other filters then decide whether that ever gets reached, and they are why the shape reads as safe:

  - `BACKTICK_PATH_RE` at `:34` only captures a span containing a known extension (`rs|md|proto|toml|sh|sql|yaml|yml|json`), so a brace group in a bare *directory* citation — `crates/{ac,gc,mc}-test-utils/` — is never captured at all.
  - `is_in_scope_path()` at `:89` admits only `docs/`, `crates/`, `proto/`, `scripts/`, so identical citations under `infra/`, `packages/` or `.claude/` are skipped regardless. In-tree today: 19 brace-with-extension citations under `infra/` and 2 under `.claude/`, all passing.

  So the guard fires in exactly one narrow window — brace group in a path segment, followed by a known extension, under one of four roots, no `*` anywhere — and passes on every neighbouring shape an author would reasonably generalise from. **Correction to the framing this was filed under**: @operations observed that `.claude/skills/{devloop,close-story,user-story,debate}/SKILL.md` is not flagged and read it as a path-resolution asymmetry. It is not — `.claude/` is simply outside the four-root allowlist, the same reason `infra/` is skipped. The asymmetry is `is_in_scope_path`'s scope, not brace handling. (Their companion claim that the guard exits 0 while printing `STATUS=FAIL` does **not** hold — measured `EXIT=1` on a violation and `EXIT=0` clean; the 0 was a pipe artifact. Recorded so it is not re-derived.)

  **Fix shape**: expand a single top-level brace group and test each expansion, rather than asking authors to hand-flatten. The tempting one-line alternative — add `{` to `is_glob_or_placeholder` — is strictly worse: it silences the one case the guard currently catches without checking anything, converting a noisy control into an inert one, which is the failure mode already recorded twice in this file. Owner: code-reviewer (owns `dt-guard` per the CLAUDE.md domain table).

- [ ] **The org concurrent-meeting cap is advisory, not enforced, under concurrent statements (2026-08-14)**: Spin-out accepted at Gate 1 of devloop `docs/devloop-outputs/2026-08-14-gc-meeting-refusal-causes/main.md` (@security S-6, owner @database, co-signed @security; Lead ruled it out of that diff's scope). `MeetingsRepository::create_meeting_with_limit_check` executes its count and its INSERT in one statement, which removes the *application-level* check-then-insert window — there is no separate `SELECT` round trip during which the count can change. It does **not** serialise concurrent executions of that statement: under READ COMMITTED the `current_count` CTE takes no row locks and no constraint enforces the cap, so N concurrent creates against a cap of M can overshoot to M+N-1. The module doc comment previously claimed the CTE "prevents TOCTOU race on concurrent meeting limit"; that claim has been corrected in-tree to state exactly the above, so this entry tracks the behaviour, not a lie in the source.

  **Scope the fix as the pattern, not this call site.** `crates/gc-service/src/repositories/participants.rs:38` and `:84` both name `create_meeting_with_limit_check` as the model for the future join-capacity CTE, so that CTE will inherit the same race for **participant** capacity — where an overshoot matters materially more than a soft meeting-count limit (a room over its participant cap is a media-plane problem, not a billing one).

  **Why it was not fixed opportunistically**: every option serialises meeting creation per-org and carries throughput/deadlock consequences that want measuring rather than guessing — `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on the org row, `SERIALIZABLE` isolation with retry, or a per-org advisory lock. That is a database-domain decision with a load profile attached.

  **Note for whoever picks this up**: the cap test cluster in `crates/gc-service/tests/meeting_create_tests.rs` (cap exhaustion, `'active'`-status counting, cross-tenant scoping) drives **sequentially** and therefore exercises the cap *value*, never its enforcement under concurrency. A green cap suite is not evidence the cap holds under load; the source carries the same warning at the cluster. Owner: database (co-signed security). Defer trigger: the join-capacity CTE landing, or any report of an org exceeding `max_concurrent_meetings`.

- [ ] **175 bare `#[allow(...)]` suppressions workspace-wide carry no `reason` attribute — ADR-0002's justification requirement is unenforced (2026-08-14)**: Surfaced at Gate 3 of devloop `docs/devloop-outputs/2026-08-14-gc-meeting-refusal-causes/main.md` by @code-reviewer; **pre-existing, not introduced by that diff**. ADR-0002 §"Suppressing Lints with `#[expect]`" requires suppressions to explain themselves at the suppression (checklist: "Each `#[expect]` has a `reason` attribute explaining why"). `grep -rn '#\[allow(' crates/*/src --include=*.rs | grep -v reason` returns **175** hits; that devloop's `errors.rs` fix is the **only** use of `reason =` with `allow` anywhere in `crates/`.

  **`reason` works on `allow`, not just `expect`** — stabilised with `lint_reasons` in Rust 1.81, and this workspace is on 1.95 (verified by compiling `#[allow(dead_code, reason = "…")]` under `#![deny(dead_code)]`). So the ADR's intent is achievable everywhere `#[expect]` is unavailable, and "we had to use `allow`" is not a reason to drop the justification. `#[expect]` genuinely cannot be used in several of these: a service crate whose `main.rs` re-declares its modules privately gets the lint firing for the bin target but not the lib, so an enum-wide `#[expect]` is unfulfilled in the lib build and warns there instead — that is the situation the GC `errors.rs` fix documents, and it will recur.

  **Why it is worth closing rather than knowing.** A bare `#[allow]` is textually identical whether it was reasoned about or pasted, so a `grep` for unjustified suppressions cannot rank them and a reviewer must reconstruct each argument from scratch. Roughly **11 of GC's 27** have no justification in *any* form — not even a trailing `//` — including `services/mc_assignment.rs`, `repositories/meeting_assignments.rs` (×2), `repositories/media_handlers.rs`, `services/mc_client.rs`, `models/mod.rs`, and the `#[allow(unused_imports)]` pairs in `repositories/mod.rs` (×3) and `services/mod.rs` (×2). Of those that do carry a comment, several assert a future that has since arrived or been abandoned — `// Will be used in Phase 2+`, `// Will be used in Phase 3 for scope checking`, `// Will be used in future phases` (×3) — which is the same decay the GC fix found on the `GcError` enum, where a blanket `#[allow(dead_code)]` labelled "Variants will be used in Phase 2+" had been suppressing nothing for the library for an unknown length of time while masking all fifteen variants.

  **Shape of the fix**: mechanical pass adding `reason = "…"` to every `#[allow]`, converting to `#[expect]` wherever the lint genuinely fires for all targets (which makes it self-retiring), and deleting the ones whose stated future has arrived — the last category is the valuable one and is only discoverable by attempting the conversion, since an `#[expect]` that turns out unfulfilled is the compiler telling you the suppression is dead. Best done per-crate to keep review tractable; GC and AC are the densest. A follow-on guard asserting every `#[allow]` in `crates/*/src` carries a `reason` would keep it from re-accumulating, and belongs with that work rather than before it. Owner: code-reviewer (ADR-0002 policy) + each service specialist for their crate. Defer trigger: the `clippy::pedantic` workspace consolidation below, which will surface a fresh backlog of suppressions and is the natural moment to set the convention.

## Test Debt

### `bcrypt_metrics_integration.rs` advertises a bucket-fidelity assertion it does not contain (2026-09-09, story task #22)

**Owner**: `test` + `auth-controller`. **Task-sized, not a one-liner.**

`crates/ac-service/tests/bcrypt_metrics_integration.rs`'s doc comment advertises a
histogram-bucket-fidelity assertion and describes `DEFAULT_BCRYPT_COST` as load-bearing
for the 50 ms–1000 ms bucket design. **The test bodies do not contain that assertion** —
they assert observation counts and unobserved/adjacency only, and nothing reads a bucket.
So `DEFAULT_BCRYPT_COST` is a production constant whose lowering would move timings
outside the designed bucket range **with no failing test**, while the file reads as
though that case were covered.

**Why it is task-sized rather than a one-line fix**:
`crates/common/src/observability/testing.rs` has **no bucket introspection at all** — only
observation-count assertions. Proving that observations land in the designed range needs a
new method on `MetricAssertion`, a helper shared by every service, so the change is a
shared-test-infrastructure change with four consumers, not an edit to one test.

**Contrast, so the two are not conflated**: story task #22's bucket-objective binding in
`mh-service` (`MEDIA_FORWARD_OBJECTIVE_SECONDS` ∈ `MEDIA_FORWARD_LATENCY_BUCKETS`) is a
pure **constant-membership** assertion — it checks that a named constant equals one of the
declared bucket edges, needs no introspection of recorded observations, and is not
evidence that this gap is closed.

- [ ] **Several `scripts/**/*.test.sh` have no invocation site — and a grep cannot tell you which (2026-08-13)**: Accepted deferral recorded by @test at Gate 3 of devloop `docs/devloop-outputs/2026-08-13-run-story-seams-and-hermetic-tests/main.md` (M3). There is no `*.test.sh` auto-runner, so an unwired self-test passes by never executing. Verified 2026-08-13: `find scripts -name '*.test.sh'` → 16; filtering to real execution sites → **6**, all in `scripts/layer3.sh`. The other ten were: `scripts/lang/_common.test.sh`, `_dispatch.test.sh`, `_get_base_ref.test.sh`, `_get_base_ref.behavior-equivalence.test.sh`, `_layer_skeleton.test.sh`, `_wrapper_trap.test.sh`, `scripts/lang/proto/changed.test.sh`, `scripts/lang/rust/changed.test.sh`, `scripts/lang/rust/behavior-equivalence.test.sh`, `scripts/lang/ts/changed.test.sh`. **UPDATE 2026-08-20 (validation-run-all): the three `changed.test.sh` (proto/rust/ts) were DELETED with the `changed.sh` classifier (ADR-0033 §2/§3), so the inventory is now 13 files, of which 7 remain unwired** (drop the three `changed.test.sh` from the list above). Re-`find` before acting; the point stands with the smaller set.

  **Why a convention cannot close this**: a mention is indistinguishable from an invocation to a grep. All ten are name-dropped in this file, ADR-0033 and the `docs/specialist-knowledge/*/INDEX.md` files, so the naive check a maintainer would actually reach for returns "referenced, looks fine" for every one of them. That is what makes the gap durable rather than merely present, and it is the argument for a guard over a convention.

  **Home is already built**: `crates/dt-guard/src/test_registration.rs` solves the identical failure class in the other language — its doc comment is this entry's sentence with `crates/*/tests/<subdir>/*.rs` swapped for `scripts/**/*.test.sh` ("Catches the common mistake of adding a test file in a subdirectory without registering it — those tests silently don't run"). Rule-id plumbing, `Finding`/`explain` output and guard-runner wiring all exist. Scope this as **"add a second scope to an existing guard"**, not "design a new guard".

  **Decision the follow-up must make, not default**: full triage of all ten (each is plausibly superseded rather than forgotten, and wiring them all has a runtime cost against ADR-0033 §4's 90s always-run budget) versus a frozen-baseline ratchet that reds only on new arrivals. The ratchet delivers the "don't add an 11th" mechanism immediately but institutionalizes the ten, which sits against CLAUDE.md §Fail loudly; never mask. @test leans ratchet-with-expiry on the `audit-suppressions.toml` precedent — this repo's existing answer to exactly that tension — but it is a real decision.

  **Generalize the acceptance criterion beyond "has an invocation site."** The devloop that produced this entry found a *wired, executing* case that was still vacuous, and named the class better than "unrun test" does: **a case whose expected outcome is also the outcome of the mechanism never running.** Its `h3` asserted `assert_absent '"decision":"block"'` against `devloop-stop-hook.sh` — satisfied equally by the hook allowing the stop, by the hook erroring, and by the hook not existing. Measured: with the hook repointed at a nonexistent path, `h3` PASSED while its sibling `h2` caught the deletion. The repair was to assert **both halves of the contract** the hook documents at `devloop-stop-hook.sh:11` ("Exit 0 with no output = allow"), which is what distinguishes "allowed" from "never ran". Two consequences for this entry: (a) the sweep that finds these must be **mechanical, not argued** — `h3` was outside the predicted-vacuous subset, which is the whole case for sweeping; (b) **`scripts/layer7.test.sh` is the known instance to check next** — it installs a fake `dev-cluster` at `:57-77` that drops no ran-marker, so across 469 lines no case can distinguish "the path I meant to test ran" from "another path produced the same status".

  **Base rate, measured in one gate.** Four defects in the devloop that produced this entry were found only by *executing* a lane, never by reading it, and all four had been read and approved by multiple reviewers: OPS-1 (removing `|| true` unmasked a write failure, but a bare `jq >"$rec"` under `set -e` then aborted before the loud message could print — the repair had made the report unreachable); the `find`-exit silent lane; case `h`'s blind assertion; and OPS-4 (`--stop-after` falsely refusing any task with deps — verified against this repo's own story manifest, where `--stop-after=3` and `=4` both refused tasks the runner reaches normally). **A fifth was found by a case that did not exist while reading as though it did** — the suite's `E4` was a `# E4:` heading followed by a fixture restore and no `e4-` label anywhere, which is what let OPS-4 through a suite built specifically to catch untested lanes. Hence the companion rule now in `scripts/workflow/run-story.test.sh:46-52`: **a comment is not a case** — every `# En:` heading must be followed by assertions carrying that label, with the grep to check it. Any guard built for this entry should enforce that too; it is the same predicate one layer up.

  **Stated limit of the obvious technique**, so the follow-up does not over-trust it: mutation testing proves the tests you *have* are load-bearing and says nothing about the lanes you never wrote. Catching the never-written class requires enumerating lanes against the code, not reading the suite. Owner: test. To be scheduled.

- [ ] **The client SDK's `MockWebTransport` has injection and inspection but NO adverse-condition knob, so ADR-0036 §11's SDK sender-side drop counter will ship with the exact reachability gap the MH transport seam just closed (found 2026-09-01 by @test while restating the seam task in mechanism language, at Gate 1 of `docs/devloop-outputs/2026-09-01-mh-transport-seam/`; owner: client)**. `packages/test-utils/src/MockWebTransport.ts` offers `simulateIncomingDatagram`, `simulateBidiStream`, `simulateServerMessage`, `simulateClose`, `simulateError`, `getOutboundDatagrams`, `getOutboundBidiWrites` — every one of them either injects input or inspects output. **None of them makes the transport behave badly**: there is no loss knob, no send-capacity/back-pressure knob, and no delay knob. §11 assigns the SDK the sender-side drop counter in terms — "the SDK keeps the transport queue shallow, owns a bounded queue above it, makes the drop decision there, and counts it — making the drop observable by construction" — and calls that drop the one that "matters most", because it occurs in the sender and MH structurally cannot observe it. Whoever writes that counter will have no deterministic way to fire it, which is the condition `crates/mh-test-utils/src/transport_shim.rs` exists to prevent on the Rust side; `set_send_capacity` there is the shape to mirror. **Second, smaller half**: `MockWebTransport.ts:234` copies on capture (`const out = new Uint8Array(chunk.byteLength); out.set(chunk);`), so the TS side cannot assert a zero-copy property even if one were claimed — the cross-language zero-copy claim is asymmetric and neither side documents that. Note the Rust seam's fidelity boundary makes the same point in the other direction (production copies below the seam), so neither side should assume the other's guarantee. Related: @dry-reviewer's entry under §Cross-Service Duplication tracks the *shape* drift between the two doubles; this entry tracks the *capability* gap. Two limbs of one fact — the Rust and TS halves of one mechanism diverging with no compiler between them — so fixing one without the other leaves the mechanism half-built.

- [ ] **No mechanical guard stops a `*-test-utils` crate from becoming a production dependency, and one of the four is now a drop-in for a production hot-path type (raised by @security as S2 at Gate 1 of `docs/devloop-outputs/2026-09-01-mh-transport-seam/`, scoping corrected by @security and @test in the same round; owner: security for the rule, infrastructure/dt-guard for the wiring)**. **Rule, stated in matcher-unambiguous form**: a `*-test-utils` path dependency in any workspace manifest must appear only under `[dev-dependencies]`. **Baseline: zero violations today** — `ac-test-utils`, `gc-test-utils` and `mc-test-utils` are each dev-scoped in their service manifest, and the only other tree-wide hit is `crates/common/Cargo.toml`'s `[features] test-utils = [...]`, which is a feature definition rather than a dependency edge. So this lands green on day one as a pure regression guard with no cleanup attached; recording that matters, because a guard whose implementer expects it to land red gets an exemption on day one instead of a fix. **Why it is worth having despite the compiler already closing the accidental path**: `mh-test-utils` is different in kind from its three siblings — they are assertion helpers and mocks of external services, none implementing a production trait that production code is generic over, whereas `LossDelayTransport` is a lossy, delaying, capacity-refusing implementation of `mh_service::transport::MediaTransport`. Substituting it would not fail to compile; it would silently degrade media. The `[dev-dependencies]` edge makes substitution a visible one-line manifest move rather than a build-flag flip, but it is one line, not impossible. **Second member of the class, already in the tree**: wtransport's `dangerous-configuration` (certificate-validation bypass) is dev-scoped at `crates/mh-service/Cargo.toml` and `crates/mc-service/Cargo.toml`. A dev-only *feature* migrating into `[dependencies]` is the same defect as a test-utils path dep doing so, so the guard should be designed for the class rather than for one instance and widened later. **Scope, corrected — do not shelve this on a phantom cost**: an earlier draft justified deferring it as "ADR-0034 means a new dt-guard subcommand plus registration plus wrapper plus self-test plus layer wiring". That premise is false. ADR-0034 collapsed guards that *had* dt-guard subcommands into thin wrappers; it did not close the door on a small bash drift check, and five pure-bash guards invoking no dt-guard subcommand post-date its acceptance — `audit-suppressions.sh` (24 LoC), `selftest-gate2-verdict.sh` (499), `validate-story-manifest.sh` (22), `validate-subdomain-regex-sync.sh` (270), `validate-slug-class-sync.sh` (104). The real shape is **one bash guard in that established idiom plus one layer registration, ~100 LoC, copying `validate-slug-class-sync.sh`** — carrying a pinned expected count of test-utils dev-dep edges so it cannot pass vacuously when a crate is renamed, which is the anti-vacuity bar `validate-subdomain-regex-sync.sh` sets and the reason it is ~100 LoC rather than ~20. Spun out rather than fixed in the seam devloop because it is a four-crate class fix whose other three owning specialists were not in that loop.

## From ADR-0024 §6 Amendment (2026-04-18)

- [ ] **Plan-template ⟶ Layer A + Layer B guards + Gate 1 invocation + Gate 1 reviewer-checklist**: template extension already shipped. Author `validate-cross-boundary-scope.sh` (Layer A: diff vs. plan file list, runs at Gate 2) and `validate-cross-boundary-classification.sh` (Layer B: GSA-not-Mechanical + Owner-field-filled, runs at Gate 1 primarily and Gate 2 as safety net); build ownership manifest mapping GSA paths to required specialists; add Gate 1 invocation step to SKILL.md Step 5 (already drafted in amendment); add Gate 1 checklist item to `.claude/skills/devloop/review-protocol.md`. See ADR-0024 §6.8 item 1. Owners: operations + test + security + code-reviewer. Medium devloop.
- [x] **GSA sync guard** (resolved 2026-04-20): implemented as `scripts/guards/simple/validate-gsa-sync.sh`. The guard became the 5th mirror by design — canonical GSA list + INTERSECTION_SUBPATHS allowlist hardcoded in the guard; bidirectional subset checks against all 4 existing mirrors (ADR §6.4, SKILL.md, review-protocol.md, cross-boundary-ownership.yaml). Catches: canon-missing-from-mirror, mirror-count-mismatch, typo'd-stray-YAML-key, canon-ahead-of-mirrors. Only silent case is triple coordination failure (anchor-of-truth comments + human review mitigate).
- [ ] **The Cross-Boundary Classification table cannot express "deliberately not touched" (2026-08-14)**: Surfaced at Gate 2 of devloop `docs/devloop-outputs/2026-08-14-gc-meeting-refusal-causes/main.md`. `validate-cross-boundary-scope.sh` parses **every** table row as a planned file and flags plan entries the diff does not touch, so a row reading "NOT TOUCHED" is mechanically indistinguishable from a plan entry the implementer failed to fulfil. @database had specifically asked for two such rows (`migrations/**`, `.sqlx/`) so the untouched-ness was explicit rather than an omission — a reader six months out cannot distinguish "considered and deliberately excluded" from "never thought about it" when the entry simply is not there. Interim resolution: moved to a prose **"Deliberately NOT touched"** section beneath the table.

  **Durable fix: the scope guard grows a `NOT-TOUCHED` assertion.** A structured token, *not* prose. The assertion is the exact inverse of what the guard already runs — "no diff path matches this glob" versus "every table path is touched" — i.e. a set-membership test over `git diff --name-only` with **no intent-parsing anywhere**, and cheaper than the positive case. (Recorded because the first justification offered for the prose section was that a marker would force the guard to parse intent; @database corrected it, and a recommendation resting on a wrong premise gets re-litigated the first time someone checks it.)

  **Why it is worth building rather than living with the section**: prose under a heading is unparsed, so nothing stops a future devloop asserting "deliberately not touched: `migrations/**`" while its diff touches `migrations/`. That matters most precisely where it is most tempting to skip — `migrations/**` is a **Guarded Shared Area**, and untouched-ness is exactly the claim that ought to be machine-verified rather than asserted.

  **Explicit limit, so it is not overclaimed**: a `NOT-TOUCHED` assertion is **vacuously true for a glob that matches nothing**, so it would *not* catch the ADR-0024 §6.4 `db/migrations/**` dead-glob problem (that path matches zero tracked files in this repo, which uses `migrations/`). That needs the separate ≥1-tracked-file check @operations is tracking. Two different holes; this closes one. Owner: operations + database. Defer trigger: the next devloop that needs a deliberate-absence row, or the dead-glob check landing (build both together — they are the same guard).

- [ ] **ADR-0024 §6.4's schema-evolution GSA glob matches zero tracked files — the control is inert repo-wide (2026-08-14)**: Surfaced at Gate 1 of devloop `docs/devloop-outputs/2026-08-14-gc-meeting-refusal-causes/main.md` by @security and @database independently; Lead ruled it out of that diff's scope (five mirrored edits plus a guard change from inside an unrelated devloop would put a change to the *definition* of a security control into a diff nobody is reviewing for that). All five mirrors declare the path as `db/migrations/**` — ADR-0024:404, `.claude/skills/devloop/SKILL.md:134`, `.claude/skills/devloop/review-protocol.md:30`, `scripts/guards/simple/cross-boundary-ownership.yaml:44`, and the CANON array at `crates/dt-guard/src/gsa_sync.rs:40`. Ground truth: `git ls-files | grep -c '^db/migrations/'` → **0**; `'^migrations/'` → **8**. `db/migrations/` has never existed in this repo.

  **Operational consequence.** `cross-boundary-ownership.yaml:44` is what `validate-cross-boundary-classification.sh` reads to enforce the two rules in review-protocol.md:52 — GSA paths cannot be `Mechanical`, and GSA paths with a non-`Mine` classification require an Owner in the manifest. Because the glob matches nothing, **both rules are currently inert for schema evolution**: a migration can be classified `Mechanical` and land with no `Approved-Cross-Boundary: database` trailer, with every automated gate green. Schema evolution is a GSA precisely because migrations quietly change security-relevant structure — CHECK constraints, unique indexes, `ON DELETE CASCADE` behaviour — so this is a live gap in a security control, not a documentation typo.

  **Three parts to the fix, and the third is the durable one.** (1) Correct the string in all five mirrors together. (2) Add an existence assertion to the sync guard: fail if any CANON path matches zero tracked files — without it the next mirrored path typo reproduces this exactly, and the string correction alone just resets the clock. (3) Record the generalization, because this is the *third* instance found in one devloop of the same shape.

  **Why it evaded detection, which is the reusable lesson.** `validate-gsa-sync` **passes**. It compares the five mirrors against each other, and they are perfectly consistent — it has no notion of whether the path being synchronised corresponds to anything on disk. A drift guard that checks internal consistency rather than correspondence to reality is structurally blind to exactly one failure mode: every mirror being wrong in the same way. That is also the failure mode people most trust it to have excluded, which is what makes it dangerous rather than merely incomplete. Two sibling instances found in the same devloop share the shape — `guard:ignore` is silently **inert** for `no-secrets-in-logs` because `rust_log_secrets.rs` never imports `crate::ignore`, so an annotation reads as a justified suppression while suppressing nothing; and `no-secrets-in-logs` Check 4's "Category-A word anywhere on the line" test scored four false positives on message prose in `crates/gc-service/src/handlers/meetings.rs` while being blind to a real credential reachable through a derived `Debug` in the same crate (fixed under that devloop's finding S-7). **The missing predicate in all three is the same: does this control's target actually exist?** No amount of mirror-consistency, annotation-syntax, or pattern-match checking supplies it. A control that passes its own self-check while protecting nothing is worse than an absent control, because it consumes the attention that would otherwise go to building a real one. Co-signed from the semantic side by @semantic-guard, who is recording the `Debug`-reachability half as a Rust extension to Credential Leak in `scripts/guards/semantic/checks.md`.

  **On whether this needs a micro-debate**: @security's **recommendation** — recorded as a recommendation, not a decision, per Lead's Gate 1 ruling — is that it does not. ADR-0024 has already decided schema evolution is guarded; correcting a path string so an already-accepted control actually fires is repair, not extension, and the mirror comment gates *extending* the GSA list. Reading it to also gate *repairing* a broken entry leaves a dead control dead pending a debate, which inverts the purpose. The owning specialists get the final call in the devloop that does the work. Owner: operations (owns ADR-0024 §6), co-sign database (`migrations/**` is theirs). Defer trigger: the next devloop touching `migrations/`, or the `NOT-TOUCHED` assertion above landing — build both together, they are the same guard.

  **Two more instances of the identical shape — the proto-gen / build.rs GSAs (found 2026-08-21 by @protocol AND independently by @security at Gate 1 of `docs/devloop-outputs/2026-08-21-gc-invalid-request-rejection-reason/`)**: `cross-boundary-ownership.yaml:31-32` declare the wire-format GSAs as `proto-gen/**` and `build.rs`, but the real tracked paths are `crates/proto-gen/**` and `crates/proto-gen/build.rs` (`git ls-files | grep -c '^proto-gen/'` → **0**; `'^build.rs$'` → **0**; the files live under `crates/proto-gen/`). The manifest matcher is prefix-anchored (verified against `crates/dt-guard/src/manifest_match.rs` + tests), so **Layer B GSA-detection for both the proto-gen and build.rs GSAs is inert** — a proto-gen or build.rs edit can be classified `Mechanical` and land with no `Approved-Cross-Boundary: protocol` trailer, every gate green. This is what let the row-66 `crates/proto-gen/**`-as-Mechanical mislabel slip the Layer B guard in this very devloop (Lead caught it by hand; row dropped). Same root cause as the `db/migrations/**` entry above, same three-part fix — and this is now the **fourth+fifth** dead-glob instance of the shape, so part (2) (the ≥1-tracked-file existence assertion on every CANON path) is the durable fix that closes all of them at once; the per-string corrections in the 5-location §6.4 mirror just reset the clock. `validate-gsa-sync` stays green throughout because all five mirrors agree on the wrong string — the structural blindness already documented above. Note the canonical GSA text (ADR-0024 §6.4, SKILL.md, review-protocol.md) writes these as `proto/**`, `proto-gen/**`, `build.rs`; deciding whether the fix is to anchor the yaml globs to `crates/proto-gen/**` or to re-root all mirrors is itself the governance call that keeps this task-sized. Owner: operations (owns ADR-0024 §6), co-sign protocol (proto-gen/build.rs are theirs). Defer trigger: same as above — build with the existence assertion.

- [ ] **Layer B classification guard fails open on a bad `--main-md` path (found 2026-08-21 by @security at Gate 1 of `docs/devloop-outputs/2026-08-21-gc-invalid-request-rejection-reason/`)**: `scripts/guards/simple/validate-cross-boundary-classification.sh:9` forwards `--main-md "$1"` only when `-f "$1"` passes (`[[ $# -ge 1 && -f "$1" && "$1" == *.md ]]`). If the Lead passes a **typo'd** plan path at Gate 1, the `-f` test fails, the arg is silently dropped, and the guard falls through to its Gate-2 default (diff-scan) mode — reporting `STATUS=OK ... clean-N-files` for a green gate **that never read the plan**. A mistyped path at the one place a human invokes this by hand yields false assurance. The fix is fail-closed: when an argument is present but is not a readable `.md` file, error out (exit non-zero with a REASON) rather than fall through to diff-scan. ~3 lines, but it wants a self-test asserting the fail-closed behaviour (bad path → non-zero, not `STATUS=OK`), so it is a small dedicated devloop, not an inline edit inside an unrelated task — and editing the guard from within a devloop that the guard itself gates is the helper-cannot-self-validate hazard (ADR-0030 corollary). This devloop's own Gate 1 was NOT affected: the guard reported `STATUS=FAIL owner_not_in_manifest` on a real violation before passing, proving it read the plan. Owner: operations + security. Defer trigger: next devloop touching `scripts/guards/simple/` or the cross-boundary guards.

- [ ] **Light-mode reviewer-specialist coverage gap** (observed 2026-04-20 during GSA sync guard devloop): light mode spawns implementer + security + one context reviewer. If the work touches files outside both reviewer slots' domains (e.g., this devloop touched 3 code-reviewer-owned anchor-comment files with no code-reviewer in the team), those files land without owner-specialist sign-off. Operations+security covered via adjacent concerns, but strictly the cross-boundary review wasn't complete. Options: (a) upgrade to full when files-outside-reviewers condition detected; (b) auto-add code-reviewer as 4th light-mode teammate when non-light-reviewer-owned files are in scope. Not blocking; observe in 2-3 more devloops before fixing. Owner: operations + code-reviewer.
- [ ] **Cross-boundary ownership coverage beyond GSA — broader file-type ownership map** (surfaced 2026-04-20 during /close-story devloop): ADR-0024 §6 and the `cross-boundary-ownership.yaml` manifest today cover only Guarded Shared Areas (Tier 1: auth/crypto/wire/audit/migrations — narrow, high-risk). Non-GSA files touched during cross-boundary work (skills, infra, docs, agent defs, runbooks, CI, observability conventions) have no ownership map — Layer A catches scope drift, but the Owner field in the plan's Cross-Boundary Classification table is free-text with no mechanical validation.
  
  Tension observed while designing a fix: coarse ownership maps (e.g., `infra/** → infrastructure`) are cheap to maintain but misclassify service-specialist-owned artifacts (e.g., `infra/docker/prometheus/rules/mc-alerts.yaml` is MC-owned per ADR-0031, not infrastructure-owned; `.claude/agents/{name}.md` is self-owned per convention). Fine-grained maps capture correct ownership but grow maintenance cost substantially. Applying GSA rule (a) "Mechanical disallowed" to Tier 2 paths also creates friction on common legitimate service-specialist work.
  
  Options considered (not resolved):
  - Option 1/2: Two-section manifest (GSA vs Tier 2), rule (a) only for GSA. Requires Tier 2 map.
  - Option 4: Single flat manifest, rule (a) everywhere. Either high friction (coarse map) or high maintenance (fine map).
  - Option B (earlier): docs-only — rejected because guard failures would be ignored.
  
  Revisit when someone has bandwidth to think through ownership granularity + rule scope carefully. Owner: code-reviewer + operations + dry-reviewer.
- [ ] **§6.2's auto-ESCALATE clause does not distinguish an accepted upgrade from a contested one — four devloops have now had to resolve it by hand** (filed 2026-08-13 by @paired-infrastructure at @team-lead's direction, `docs/devloop-outputs/2026-08-13-run-story-seams-and-hermetic-tests/`). ADR-0024 §6.2 says reviewers may upgrade a classification "at Gate 1 or during Gate 3 review" and, in the next sentence, that "Classification challenges auto-route to ESCALATE"; `review-protocol.md` §Classification Monotonicity repeats the second half without the first. Read literally, raising an upgrade **at the gate the ADR itself prefers** forces an ESCALATED verdict even when the implementer amends on first ask — which penalises the cheap behaviour (Gate 1, before code exists) and rewards holding the concern until Gate 3, where amending is expensive.

  **Not a novel misreading — it recurs, and it has already been arbitrated once.** `docs/devloop-outputs/2026-05-23-camelcase-wire-migration/main.md:63` recorded the same ruling in-flight ("consensual classification refinement stays in normal Gate-1 flow — this is NOT a disputed challenge, so no ESCALATE route"), and `:464` filed it as a lesson learned, noting the implementer "initially over-interpreted this as ESCALATE-class". `2026-05-06-test-utils-package/main.md:82,88` carries two owner-requested upgrades handled in normal Gate-1 flow; `2026-07-29-client-credential-lifetime-guard-task58/main.md:1043` carries a @code-reviewer upgrade (*"no guard covers wrapper-registration"*) likewise. This devloop is the fourth, with five upgrades across three reviewers, and required a fresh @team-lead arbitration to reach the conclusion already recorded in 2026-05-23. **A rule that must be re-arbitrated every time it is exercised is a defect in the text, not in its readers** — the cost is paid in Lead turns and in reviewers acquiring a mild disincentive to upgrade at all.

  **Interim rule (@team-lead, 2026-08-13, binding until the text is fixed)**: ESCALATED is reserved for an upgrade that **survives to Gate 3 contested**. An upgrade raised at Gate 1 and accepted without contest is recorded in the Gate-3 Ownership Lens — raised, by whom, on what grounds, honoured at Gate 1 — and does not force the verdict. Grounds: the §Verdict Format taxonomy defines ESCALATED as "unresolved disagreement", which is the narrower and therefore governing instrument; and §Classification Monotonicity's own stated purpose is to stop owners "being argued down during fix-or-defer triage", a Gate-3 activity.

  **Fix**: one clause in ADR-0024 §6.2 distinguishing an upgrade the implementer accepts from one that survives contested, mirrored into `review-protocol.md` §Classification Monotonicity (which currently states only the auto-route). Both documents change together or the seam simply moves. ADR amendment, so it does not ride in a devloop that merely trips over it. Owner: operations + code-reviewer.

- [x] **DRY reviewer retrospective audit on Ownership Lens verdict field** (first run 2026-08-17, story `story-runner-hardening`, 4 devloops): See ADR-0024 §6.8 item 3. Findings at `docs/devloop-outputs/story-runner-hardening-story-close/ownership-lens-retrospective.md`. Headline: classification judgment was sound (10 upgrades raised by 5 reviewers, all honoured, 0 downgrades, 0 unrouted Domain-judgment rows, 0 GSA paths as Mechanical), but the *field* was recorded in 1 of 4 devloops. Three drifts filed below. Owner: dry-reviewer. Re-run at each story close.

- [ ] **The Ownership Lens verdict field has no stable header, so §6.8 item 3 cannot be run mechanically (2026-08-17)**: ADR-0024 §6.6 step 6 requires the code-reviewer's Gate-3 verdict to carry an explicit Ownership Lens field, and `.claude/skills/devloop/review-protocol.md` §Verdict Format defines the `### Ownership Lens` section. Measured across the `story-runner-hardening` story: `grep -i 'ownership lens'` hits `2026-08-13-run-story-seams-and-hermetic-tests/main.md` only. `2026-08-14`, `2026-08-15` and `2026-08-17` all record the substance — per-file classification tables, Gate-1 confirmations, Gate-3 verdict tables, and in `2026-08-17` a dedicated §Commit Trailers section — but none names the field, so the retrospective had to be reconstructed by reading §Cross-Boundary Classification and correlating it against `git interpret-trailers`.

  **The gap is venue, not diligence.** The verdict template lives in `review-protocol.md`, which governs the message a reviewer *sends*; `main.md` is written by the implementer, and its §Code Review Results is a summary the implementer composes from those messages. Nothing requires the Ownership Lens section to survive that transcription, and in three of four cases it did not. A retrospective that must reconstruct the field from primary sources is a retrospective that will not be run.

  **Fix shape (not decided here)**: require an `### Ownership Lens` subsection under §Code Review Results in the `main.md` template, quoting the code-reviewer's field verbatim rather than paraphrasing it — the same "record it where the reader looks" move `2026-08-17` made for commit trailers. A Layer-3 presence check is cheap once the header is mandatory, and would make §6.8 item 3 a grep rather than a reading exercise. Owner: code-reviewer + operations.

- [ ] **Same edit shape, two classifications: the `scripts/layer3.sh` `run_and_emit` wiring line (2026-08-17)**: One-line additions to `layer3.sh` wiring a new `*.test.sh` into the always-run gate were classified three times in one story and landed on two different tiers. `2026-08-13` filed it **Mechanical**, was **upgraded to Minor-judgment** (U-1, at the owner's request and @code-reviewer's ruling) on the grounds that ADR-0024 §6.2 requires Mechanical to be *covered by the guard pipeline* and defaults to Minor-judgment where no guard covers the file-type × change-pattern — and that same devloop's M3 established that none does. `2026-08-15` filed the identical shape **Minor-judgment**, consistent with the ruling. `2026-08-17` filed it **Mechanical** again ("explicit wiring line for the sync-guard self-test, mirroring `:44`"), and no reviewer challenged it.

  **Why the third one is a regression rather than a defensible difference.** The implementer differed (`operations` owns `layer3.sh`, so the row reads `Mine`), but ownership determines *routing*, not *tier* — U-1 turned on guard coverage of the file × change-pattern, which is unchanged. And the hazard U-1 named is unchanged too: the dangerous partial version of this edit is test file present, wiring line absent, which is silent under every gate.

  **Fix**: this is the case the Tier-2 ownership map above would settle mechanically, but it does not need to wait for one — `layer3.sh` wiring lines are a small, enumerable class. Either add the file × change-pattern to the guard pipeline (which would legitimately make it Mechanical), or record the tier once where a planner will find it. Owner: operations + code-reviewer.

- [ ] **`review-protocol.md` asks for a trailer that ADR-0024 says is optional — and the story's commits split 2/2 on it (2026-08-17)**: `review-protocol.md` §Verdict Format, Ownership Lens, asks for Minor-judgment: *"Has the owner-specialist recorded an `Approved-Cross-Boundary:` trailer for each hunk they own?"* — phrased as a precondition. ADR-0024 §6.6 says owner confirmation "is collapsed into the Gate 1 / Gate 3 review flow rather than a separate commit-time trailer-enforcement pass", and §6.7 titles trailers *Optional*. The commit-time consistency check was explicitly dropped (§6.8 Reshaped-or-dropped), so nothing detects a missing one.

  **Measured across this story's four commits**: `09a5499` (2 trailers: observability, operations) and `9d3b94b` (2: test, protocol) carry them; `33ace8d` and `d096de0` carry none. `33ace8d` is the interesting one — `2026-08-13/main.md` §Cross-Boundary Classification states *"I am taking the `ci.yml` trailer @paired-infrastructure offered, because its reason clause is where the 'closes CI only' scoping lives"*, and the trailer is not in the commit. `d096de0` carries roughly a dozen non-Mine Minor-judgment rows across four owners (`operations`, `infrastructure`, `client`, Lead) and no trailer at all. Neither is a gate failure, because by ADR-0024 neither had to be — but `2026-08-13`'s own document reads as though one landed.

  **Two independent defects, and the second is the durable one.** (1) A stated trailer that never landed is a document asserting a breadcrumb that `git log` does not have; the same devloop's §Ownership Lens reasoning cites the trailer's reason clause as where a scoping decision lives, so the decision is now recorded only in `main.md`. (2) The two documents disagree about whether the trailer is required, which is why practice is inconsistent rather than uniformly-optional: reviewers reading `review-protocol.md` ask for one, implementers reading the ADR treat it as optional, and both are correctly following their own text. ## Suppressed Advisories (mirror of audit-suppressions.toml)

Source of truth is `audit-suppressions.toml` (repo root); this is a human-readable mirror
(task #47). Suppression is ONLY ever added there via a reviewed PR (ADR-0033 §11) — never
via CLI flags, hand-edited derived files, or Dependabot alert dismissals. See
`docs/contributor/audit-suppressions.md`.

| id | ecosystem | ticket |
|----|-----------|--------|
| RUSTSEC-2023-0071 | rust | this section (Cluster C below) |
| RUSTSEC-2025-0052 | rust | 'Polyglot Pipeline Follow-ups' → async-std entry |
| GHSA-h67p-54hq-rp68 | js | this section |

> **`expires` and the exposure rationale are deliberately NOT reproduced here — read them from
> `audit-suppressions.toml`.** They used to be, and on 2026-09-02 this table was found carrying both
> a stale `expires` and a superseded rationale ("build-time-only via sqlx-macros", by then corrected
> to lockfile-only in the manifest): it had drifted from the source of truth and nothing noticed,
> because nothing checks it. Rather than add machinery to keep a hand-maintained prose mirror
> faithful, the duplicated *values* were removed — CLAUDE.md's single-source-of-truth rule offers
> "derive one from the other **or** guard the drift", and deleting the copy is the cheaper and more
> durable of the two. What stays here is the analysis that exists nowhere else (Cluster C, the GHSA
> decomposition, the MTTR-source ambiguity). **Do not re-add an `expires` or `summary` column.**

The always-run `scripts/audit-suppressions-check.sh` (Layer-3 guard) hard-fails any entry past
`expires`; the weekly `audit-scheduled.yml` scan catches new advisories against unchanged deps.

> **Known gap the above does NOT close** (surfaced by @security, 2026-09-02, verified against
> `__sync_check`): the guard's drift check builds `rust_ids`/`js_ids` from the id field alone and
> `diff`s **sorted id sets**. It never compares `expires` and never compares reason text, in any
> mirror. So `.cargo/audit.toml`'s comment block — which *does* carry the expiry and rationale — can
> be hand-edited into disagreement with the manifest and the check still passes, because the id set
> still matches. **The machinery guards the set of suppressed IDs and leaves every human-readable
> justification field unguarded, everywhere**, which is the wrong half: the id set is the part a
> reviewer never has to reason about, while `expires` and the exposure analysis are the two fields a
> renewal decision actually rests on. `--fix` keeps the derived comments honest in practice, so this
> is a latent hand-edit gap rather than an active drift. Tracked below. Owner: operations + security.

  - **Cluster C**: rsa@0.9.10 ignore in audit config with rationale (closes RUSTSEC-2023-0071). **Policy text of record** per ADR-0033 §11 (security-owned threshold + ignore-list) — verbatim TOML block authored by @security 2026-05-08, to land in `audit-config.toml` exactly as written:

    ```toml
    [[ignore]]
    id = "RUSTSEC-2023-0071"
    # Crate: rsa 0.9.10 (Marvin Attack — timing side-channel on RSA decryption)
    #
    # Exposure analysis (security, 2026-05-08):
    #   - Pulled in transitively by sqlx-macros-core's compile-time query-
    #     validation scaffolding, NOT by any runtime driver we select.
    #   - Workspace sqlx config (Cargo.toml): features = ["runtime-tokio",
    #     "postgres", "uuid", "chrono", "migrate"]. No "mysql" feature; no
    #     runtime code path constructs an rsa::* primitive.
    #   - cargo tree -p rsa --invert (verified 2026-05-08) confirms only
    #     build-time consumers; no shipped binary links rsa runtime.
    #   - Marvin Attack requires attacker-observable RSA decrypt timing on a
    #     server we operate. We don't operate one — we don't ship rsa code.
    #
    # Upstream status:
    #   - No fix available in rsa 0.9.x. Constant-time RSA primitives in Rust
    #     remain an unsolved upstream problem (see rust-lang/rsa#19, et al.);
    #     waiting for an rsa fix is waiting indefinitely.
    #
    # Sunset:
    #   - Re-evaluate by 2026-08-08 (90-day default per ADR-0033 §11 audit-
    #     config policy). Re-evaluation MUST re-verify the build-time-only
    #     claim above against the then-current Cargo.lock — if any runtime
    #     driver in our deps starts pulling rsa::*, this entry FAILS-CLOSED:
    #     remove the ignore, fix, OR re-justify with new exposure analysis.
    #   - Permanence note: this entry is expected to be the longest-lived in
    #     audit-config.toml because no upstream fix is on the horizon. That
    #     does NOT make it unconditional — the build-time-only invariant is
    #     the load-bearing claim, and that invariant must be re-checked at
    #     each sunset.
    ```

    Operational substance preserved alongside the TOML block:

    - **Verification command of record**: `cargo tree -p rsa --invert` is the command for re-verifying the build-time-only invariant at each sunset/tripwire fire.
    - **90-day sunset** (re-evaluate by **2026-09-01** — re-anchored to the manifest-landing date when task #47 created `audit-suppressions.toml`; the original 2026-08-08 figure was computed from the 2026-05-08 authoring date, before the manifest existed, and is now stale): heavy active re-justification — re-run `cargo tree -p rsa --invert`, confirm runtime tree is still empty, re-affirm in-tree that the rationale still holds. The mechanical teeth are the manifest `expires = "2026-09-01"`, enforced by the always-run `scripts/audit-suppressions-check.sh`.
    - **Fail-closed condition** (also encoded in the TOML rationale): if any runtime driver starts pulling `rsa::*`, the ignore expires immediately — no extension, no grace period.
    - **ADR-0033 §12 14-day MTTR tripwire continues to apply** per security's explicit decision; no special-casing. **Tripwire vs sunset** distinction: tripwire = light periodic re-verification of "still build-time-only, still no fix" (cargo tree + advisory-db check); sunset = heavy active re-justification (full rationale review). Both fire, both add value, they do not conflict.
    - Cluster C is **expected to be the longest-lived entry** in `audit-suppressions.toml`. The rationale block anchors that expectation so the 2026-09-01 re-justification reads as routine active maintenance, not process failure.
