## Guard Coverage Gap — a citation whose target does not exist passes every guard (@observability, devloop 2026-09-02-mc-kek-identity-sender-id)

- [ ] **Nothing in the validation pipeline resolves a citation INTO `docs/TODO.md`, or into any document section — prose can cite an entry that does not exist and every layer stays green (owner: infrastructure, as guard machinery; policy input from observability + security as the specialists whose docs carry the most citations; trigger: the next `dt-guard` citation-family or `todo-tracking` change, or the next devloop that files a deferral citing a TODO section)**: `todo-tracking` validates the *shape* of entries in this file and the single-canonical-TODO discipline; it never looks at inbound references. **Not hypothetical and not one slip — one devloop hit the shape four times**: `docs/observability/label-taxonomy.md` §Enforcement reality and the `sender_id` comment block in `crates/dt-guard/src/common/pii_vocabulary.rs` both cited a §Observability Debt entry that did not exist; `docs/runbooks/mc-deployment.md`'s TEMPORARY item cited a §Media Path Obligations entry that never existed; and the F4/F5 pair in that loop's own record is the same mechanism one level up. Every one was caught by a **human reviewer reading the citation against the filesystem**, which is exactly the "not by review" state ADR-0036 §11's coverage-demonstration section warns about. **Record it as one gap in the guard set, not as N authoring mistakes** — the authors were careful and it still happened four times, which is the signature of a missing mechanical check rather than of carelessness. **The gap is narrower than "citations aren't checked", which is what makes it fixable**: `dt-guard cite-symbol-resolves` (Guard C) already verifies `<path>::<symbol>` cites resolve in a target file, and `cite-no-line-numbers` (Guard A) forbids bare `<path>:<line>` cites. So a citation naming a **code symbol** is checked and a citation naming a **document section** is not. The fix is an extension to an existing guard family, not a new mechanism. **Shape if built**: resolve every `docs/TODO.md` §section + entry-title reference appearing in `crates/**`, `docs/**` and `infra/**` against this file's actual headings, and fail on an unresolvable one; start with `docs/TODO.md` section names, since this is the tree's designated home for deferred work and therefore the highest-value referent. **Known design tension to settle first**: entry titles are prose and get edited, so a naive exact-match check converts a real class of *silent* rot into *noisy* rot — the citation format may need to become a stable anchor rather than a title quote. That is a decision, not an implementation detail. **Shared predicate with the sibling section below** — *a reference is an input and must be asserted present; target absent is a hard error, never a silent pass* — which is the same rule that section states for path roots and globs; whoever fixes either should read both, since one "assert the referent exists" mechanism plausibly covers reference kinds the two entries treat separately. **Why this class is worse than an ordinary stale link**: the citation is what makes the *citing* text safe to ship. Landed prose saying "this gap is tracked" reads as coverage to the next author, who then does not file it — the dangling pointer actively suppresses the filing it claims already happened. In the first occurrence above the suppressed item was a guard-inertness trigger, i.e. a control about controls. **State plainly until it is built: no guard covers this, and a "tracked in `docs/TODO.md`" claim in this repository is unverified prose.** *(Filed independently and concurrently by @observability and @meeting-controller at Gate 3; merged here as the single canonical entry.)*
  **TWO FORMS, AND THE SECOND IS STRICTLY HARDER TO CATCH (added 2026-09-08 at Gate 3 of `docs/devloop-outputs/2026-09-08-mh-datagram-receive-path-gap/`; form 2 found by @observability while fixing an instance of form 1, class unification by @dry-reviewer).**

  **Form 1 — dangling: the target does not exist.** A citation names a file, heading or anchor never written or since removed. Detectable by an existence check; this is the form the entry above was filed about.

  **Form 2 — mis-coordinated: the target exists, but not where the citation says.** The cited file exists, the cited heading exists, and the concept appears somewhere in the document — so **every check available to a reviewer or a guard returns green** — while the reader lands in a large unrelated section with no signal they are in the wrong place. Instance: `docs/observability/metrics/mh-service.md` cited "§Observability Debt" for a follow-up that lives under §Media Path Obligations. An existence check cannot see this; only a check that resolves the citation to a **specific entry** can.

  **Root cause common to both: the citation names a coordinate in a namespace the citing file does not own.** Section headings, scenario numbers and list positions are owned by the *target* document and get re-ordered, renamed and renumbered by authors who cannot see who points at them. `infra/services/mh-service/configmap.yaml` reserved "Scenario 15" in a runbook sequence it did not own and the slot was taken by an unrelated scenario; that hunk's own diagnosis — *the failure was not the pointer going stale, it was reserving a position in a sequence this file does not own* — applies unchanged to a heading.

  **Remedy: cite by a token that is stable and unique in the target, not by position.** A requirement id (`R-15`), an entry title, or a symbol name survives re-sectioning and renumbering and is greppable — which means a check **could** resolve it. **A position citation is unresolvable by construction, so no guard can ever be written for it**; that is what makes "cite by stable token" a design rule rather than a style preference, and it is the actionable half of this entry. Where only a heading is available, link from the target side, where a guard can see it.

  **The class is broader than citations — it is ANY hand-restated coordinate**: an integer, an ordinal, a section heading, a scenario number. Each rots when the thing it describes is changed by someone who cannot see the copy, and none is covered. This one devloop produced five instances across four surfaces: two dangling/mis-coordinated citations, a restated cardinality integer (`19 = 11 MH-local + 8 codec`), a reserved scenario number, and two rustdoc sentences promising "a twelfth value" would be a compile error after `ALL` had grown to thirteen. **Compile-checked lengths (`ALL: [Self; N]`) are the counter-example that shows the remedy works** — that coordinate cannot rot, because the compiler owns it.

## Review Coverage Gap — every control binds to an ARTIFACT, so a claim split across two conversations has no reader at all (owner: `infrastructure` for the review-protocol machinery, with `code-reviewer` for the scope rule; surfaced 2026-09-08 by @dry-reviewer at Gate 3 of `docs/devloop-outputs/2026-09-08-mh-datagram-receive-path-gap/`)

- [ ] **Every control in the Agent Teams review model binds to an artifact in the diff — and a claim an agent states only in outbound messages is in no artifact, so it is in no one's review scope by construction.** Guards walk files. Hunk-ACKs and `Approved-Cross-Boundary:` trailers attach to commits. The Cross-Boundary Classification table has a row per *path*. Reviewers are assigned by *domain over the diff*. Every one of those binds to something written down in the tree.
  **The gap**: no agent sees another agent's outbound messages. So when one agent states the same rule, predicate or definition to two different audiences, the two statements have no common reader, and nothing in the protocol can notice them diverging. The panel is structurally blind to it — not under-resourced, blind.
  **Concrete instance, and it is what surfaced this.** At Gate 3 of the devloop above, @dry-reviewer stated the Class A predicate for the hand-restated-coordinate taxonomy two ways: *"a coordinate in a namespace the citing file does not own"* to @observability, and the weaker *"correct when written, invalidated by an edit elsewhere"* to @implementer and @main. The weaker form silently excluded a member (F2, a citation that was never correct and therefore never rotted). It was caught only because @implementer re-ran the classification test on all eight instances himself rather than accepting the reviewer's conclusion — i.e. by an act of supererogation, not by any control.
  **Why this is NOT the citation class above.** That one is a value restated in an artifact with nothing checking the copy; the remedy is to let a compiler or guard own the coordinate, and it survives inattention. This one has **no artifact to check at all**, so no mechanism is available even in principle. Its only control is a reviewer choosing to verify a peer's claim against its source — a practice, which degrades exactly when review attention is scarce. Do not fold the two: the first one's tractable remedy would imply coverage of this one, and it provides none.
  **Note the classification is contingent, not intrinsic.** If a rule stated across two conversations were captured in an artifact — a plan section, a devloop-output row, a scratch record of reviewer-stated predicates — the same failure would become mechanically checkable and would move into the citation class. **The class boundary here tracks the artifact landscape, not the shape of the mistake**, which is worth knowing before anyone tries to fix this by re-taxonomising rather than by creating the artifact.
  **Candidate remedies, none costed, deliberately not chosen here**: (a) require that a reviewer's cross-cutting *definitions* — as opposed to per-finding comments — land in the devloop output where every panel member reads them, making them an artifact and therefore reviewable; (b) have the Lead echo any predicate a reviewer states to more than one recipient back into `main.md`; (c) accept the gap explicitly and record that the only control is the one-hop-upstream review move, so it is at least a named expectation rather than an accident. **(c) is the honest floor and costs nothing**; (a) is the one that would actually close it.
  **Do not read this as an argument for fewer reviewer conversations.** The cross-talk is what produced every real finding in that devloop; the defect is that its *conclusions* have no home, not that it happened.

## Review Coverage Gap — the Cross-Boundary table's unit is a PATH, but a path can have several authors in one changeset (owner: `infrastructure` for the table's shape, with `code-reviewer` for the Gate 1 check; surfaced 2026-09-08 by @dry-reviewer at Gate 3 of `docs/devloop-outputs/2026-09-08-mh-datagram-receive-path-gap/`)

- [ ] **The Cross-Boundary Classification table asserts one classification and one Owner per PATH, and has no vocabulary for a file several agents write to within one changeset.** `docs/TODO.md` in the surfacing devloop ended up carrying entries from **four** authors under a row reading `Mine` — @implementer's R-15 deletion and filings, @observability's at `:725` and `:2055-2064`, @dry-reviewer's at `:2066` and this entry.
  **How it survived a correctly-performed Gate 1.** The reviewer verified row **coverage** — every modified path has a row — which is static and confirmable once, at plan time. Row **correctness under changing authorship** is dynamic: it is only checkable at verdict time, after other reviewers have filed. **Nothing in the protocol asks for that check.** So the row was true when written, falsified by later writes, and re-read by nobody. The failure is in the check's *unit*, not in its execution — the Gate 1 review was performed correctly and still could not have caught this.
  **The asymmetry that makes it worth filing rather than noting**: "the reviewer confirmed the table" reads as stronger assurance than it is. A reader takes it as *the ownership claims are true*; it establishes only *no path is missing a row*.
  **Guaranteed to recur — it is manufactured by the process, not stumbled into.** The review protocol *sends* every reviewer into `docs/TODO.md` at verdict time ("tracking is the reviewer's responsibility at verdict time"), so a multi-author `docs/TODO.md` row is the **normal case** in any devloop with more than one filed finding, not an accident of this one.
  **DO NOT FOLD into `## Review Coverage Gap — every control binds to an ARTIFACT` immediately above.** They share a surface and will read as one finding. That one is about a claim with **no artifact to bind to**, where no mechanism is available even in principle. This one is about an **existing artifact whose unit is too coarse**, where the mechanism exists and its granularity is wrong. Different remedies: one needs an artifact created, the other needs an existing artifact's unit made finer.
  **The class generalises past this table — a control whose unit does not match the extent of the thing it asserts about.** Second in-tree instance, live and unguarded: `dt-guard alert-rules-policy` validates that a `runbook_url` **file** exists while the citation resolves to an **anchor**, across all 14 alerts in `infra/docker/prometheus/rules/mh-alerts.yaml` (anchors all resolve today; the convention is what is unguarded). One instance sits in a review artifact and one in a guard — same shape, different machinery, which is what makes this a class rather than a description of one devloop.
  **Third instance, and it runs the OPPOSITE direction — recorded as a sibling rather than folded in, because the direction matters.** @security's SEC-6 in the surfacing devloop: a Gate 1 wording condition (cite the constant by name, never restate the integer) was applied by @implementer to their own plan text and `main.md` and never carried to the specialists who then wrote the shipped artifacts — three instances survived in files @implementer does not own, two in @observability's catalog and one in @operations' alert annotation, each found only when its owner swept their own file after being told the class existed. The table case above is a unit too **coarse** (path vs. hunk); SEC-6 is a unit too **narrow** (one owner's files vs. a class spanning owners). Both are unit/extent mismatches and belong in one family; they are not the same defect and a single remedy will not close both. **What SEC-6 adds that the other two do not**: the per-owner sweep *works* once someone names the class — what has no owner is **the naming and the fan-out**. Nothing in the protocol assigns a class-wide sweep to anyone.
  **Candidate remedies, none costed**: (a) per-hunk or per-entry authorship in the table for shared filing surfaces; (b) a named **shared filing surface** classification whose semantics are "several owners, each owning their own entries", removing the need to assert a false single owner; (c) a verdict-time re-read of rows for any path a reviewer wrote to. **(c) is the honest floor** and closes the specific instance at near-zero cost without changing the table's shape; **(b) is the smallest change that makes the row *expressible*** — that distinction is the useful part for whoever picks this up. The SEC-6 sibling needs a different remedy again: an owner for class-wide fan-out when a Gate 1 condition names a class rather than a site.

## Guard Coverage Gaps — path roots and globs that resolve to nothing (@security S16/S17, devloop 2026-09-01-internal-contract-reshape)

**Predicate covering both entries below**: *a guard's path roots and path globs are
inputs and must be asserted present; "path absent" is a hard error, never an empty
result set.* **The assertion is the load-bearing deliverable; the path corrections
are what falls out of running it once.** A corrective rewrite alone leaves the next
drift undetected and reads as *more* trustworthy for having been recently audited.

**Diagnostic for finding further instances is consumer polarity, not usage counting.**
Being *exercised* does not protect a path root. Where some consumer reads an empty
result as a failure, a broken root fails loudly and self-corrects; where every
consumer reads empty as "nothing to check", there is no corrective. An audit asking
"is this root used?" clears every instance below.

### S16 — ADR-0024 §6.4 GSA canon: 7 of 14 enumerable globs match nothing

Measured with the guard's own matcher (`crates/dt-guard/src/common/manifest_match.rs::path_matches_glob`;
trailing `/**` is a prefix match).

**Class A — the protected concern exists at a different path. Live gap: edits draw no owner today.**

| Dead glob | Where the concern actually lives |
|---|---|
| `crates/ac-service/src/token/**` | `services/token_service.rs`, `handlers/internal_tokens.rs` |
| `db/migrations/**` | `migrations/` — 8 live SQL files. `CLAUDE.md:22` has contradicted the canon all along |
| `crates/common/src/webtransport/**` | `crates/mc-service/src/webtransport/`, `crates/mh-service/src/webtransport/` |
| `proto-gen/**` | `packages/proto-gen/`, `crates/proto-gen/` |
| `build.rs` | `crates/proto-gen/build.rs` — holds the `skip_debug` credential-redaction list |

**Class B — genuinely aspirational, no such code exists yet. Benign; do NOT rewrite uniformly with Class A.**
`crates/ac-service/src/jwks/**` (JWKS serving is `handlers/jwks_handler.rs`);
`crates/ac-service/src/audit/**` (no `audit` directory exists anywhere).

**Alive and correct**: `proto/**`, `crates/media-protocol/**`, the four
`crates/common/src/*.rs` entries, `crates/ac-service/src/crypto/**`. **`proto/**`
matches `proto/dark_tower/internal/v1/internal.proto`, so the 2026-09-01
internal-contract-reshape devloop's own three-owner intersection determination rests
on a live entry.**

**Live instance inside that devloop's own diff**: BOTH its GSA rows —
`packages/proto-gen/scripts/verify-codegen.sh` and `crates/proto-gen/tests/internal_roundtrip.rs` —
are classified GSA:YES under `proto-gen/**`, a glob matching nothing. They are inside a
Guarded Shared Area *only* because the implementer applied the §6.4 criterion by hand;
the Layer B guard would have read ordinary paths with no owner requirement.

**Why nothing caught it.** `gsa_sync.rs` has exactly three rules — `canon_missing`,
`count_mismatch`, `stray_yaml_key` — all comparing the five mirrors against *each
other*, with no filesystem access. Five synchronised copies of a dead glob is a clean
run. Sharper: the module **fails closed correctly on its own inputs** (`:221`, `:234`
push a hit when a mirror file is missing) roughly 200 lines below the `CANON` array it
never resolves. It distinguishes its *inputs* from the *content it validates* and
applies the polarity rule only to the first. And `CANON_MISSING_RULE_ID` is
**overloaded** — `:127`/`:142`/`:191` mean "a string absent from a mirror document",
`:223`/`:236` mean "a filesystem path that does not exist" — so a reader who has seen
this guard fire `canon_missing` on an absent file has *observed* the id covering
missing paths and will generalise. The module's own emitted behaviour teaches the
wrong inference.

**Additional structural gap** (verified, @implementer): `owner_not_in_manifest`
requires exact single-specialist equality, so a multi-owner Owner cell is rejected —
including for `proto/dark_tower/internal/v1/internal.proto`, the one path whose
manifest entry exists to name three owners. The guard therefore *structurally cannot*
evidence an intersection-rule co-sign.

**Fix — both halves, assertion first**: add a per-entry "matches ≥1 extant path, else
fail" assertion beside `validate-gsa-sync.sh`, then correct the drifted Class A paths.
Note the CANON array is itself one of the five mirrors, so a corrective rewrite touches
five files and the sync guard would pass on a typo.

**Method and its blind spot**: found by running each canon glob through the guard's own
matcher. That finds globs matching *nothing*; it would **not** find a glob resolving to
the *wrong live path*, which is the more dangerous variant since it reads as coverage
with a real file behind it. Enumeration is therefore partial.

**Owners**: security + auth-controller (Class A includes token issuance and the
credential-redaction list) + the guard-family owner for the assertion. **To be
scheduled — no slug.**

### S16b — `dt-guard` path roots unasserted (latent; @observability)

`application_metrics.rs:176` (`ALERTS_SUBDIR`) and `kustomize.rs:145` are
**feedback-free**: every consumer reads an empty set as success. `kustomize.rs:145` is
the sharper one — `if !dashboards.is_dir() || !kustomization.is_file() { return Ok(hits) }`
is OR-gated on two inputs so losing either silences it, one input is a single *file*,
it silences a *bidirectional* check, and the paths are inline literals with no constant
to grep. Polarity-safe ride-alongs that should get the assertion anyway:
`application_metrics.rs:66` (catalog) and `:116` (dashboards), whose checks 5/6 read
empty as "every metric undocumented/undashboarded" and scream.

**Latent, not live**: all 12 hardcoded path roots across 10 guard modules resolve today.
Distinct in urgency from S16.

**In-tree precedent for the correct pattern**: `metric_coverage.rs:66-67` documents why
its empty case is safe. The right answer has been three modules away the whole time.

**Method and its blind spot**: found by grepping `if !x.is_dir() { return }`, so
`exists()`, `try_exists()`, `match` on a read result, and `let Ok(..) else` are
invisible to it. Unassessed root-path guards: `knowledge_index.rs:203`,
`cite_extract.rs:368`/`:461`, `todo_tracking.rs:157`/`:165`, `histogram_buckets.rs:86`,
`kustomize.rs:88`/`:249`, `ts_dev_trust.rs:44`, `grafana_datasources.rs:290`/`:295`.
`cross_boundary_classification.rs:233` is explicitly **unassessed, not counted** — it
iterates diff paths where a missing path is plausibly a deletion.

**One more instance, found 2026-09-07 by @dry-reviewer and NOT caught by either method
above** — it is neither an `if !x.is_dir() { return }` nor an unassessed root, but an
*explicit, commented, deliberate* fail-open: `crates/dt-guard/src/ts_metric_naming.rs:345-348`
derives `any_target_present` from its `SCOPE_PREFIXES` roots
(`packages/sdk-core/src/`, `packages/web-app/src/`) and exits **clean** when neither
resolves, under the comment "Scaffold-now / fire-later: if neither target package exists
yet, exit clean." That was correct when the packages did not exist; both exist today, so
the rationale has expired while the code has not. It belongs in this entry's inventory
because it is the same polarity — absence reads as success — and it is the **harder**
variant to find: a reviewer grepping for missing assertions skips it, since it *has* one.
The tell is not "is there a presence check" but "what does the check do when it fails".

**REFERENCE IMPLEMENTATION NOW EXISTS** (2026-09-07, devloop
`2026-09-07-media-telemetry-deny-guard`): `crates/dt-guard/src/common/scope.rs`
`assert_scope_live(repo_root, &[rel_roots], extensions) -> Result<Vec<ScopeRoot>, Vec<ScopeFailure>>`.
It was written for `media_telemetry_deny`, the first guard whose *purpose* is this
assertion, and its signature is shaped for the general case rather than that guard's
manifest — a single hardcoded root calls it with a one-element slice and no wrapper.
It returns ALL failures rather than the first, and its `ScopeFailure` variants carry
distinct token suffixes (`scope-directory-missing` / `-empty` /
`-escapes-root` / `scope-no-directories-configured`), which is this entry's
token-overloading point applied: `gsa_sync.rs`'s `CANON_MISSING_RULE_ID` means both
"string absent from a mirror" and "path does not exist", and the module's own emitted
behaviour teaches the wrong inference. `ScopeRoot` is a newtype with no public
constructor, so a walker taking `&[ScopeRoot]` structurally cannot be pointed at an
unvalidated path.

**The 12 roots above were deliberately NOT re-pointed in that devloop** — @main scoped
it to "write the predicate, consume it here only", because re-pointing ten modules is
this entry's task and its owner's call, not a ride-along. Doing so should now be
mechanical.

**Owner**: observability (own row) + guard-family owner. **To be scheduled — no slug.**

### S17 — `rust_log_secrets` accepts a bare `guard:ignore` with no justification

`crates/dt-guard/src/rust_log_secrets.rs:135-140`:

```rust
fn is_allowed_line(line: &str) -> bool {
    line.contains("REDACTED") || line.contains("[REDACTED]")
        || line.contains("skip_all") || line.contains("// guard:ignore")
}
```

Bare substring. No reason extraction, no `is_lazy_reason()`, no `MIN_REASON_LEN`. So
`tracing::info!("token={}", token); // guard:ignore` fully suppresses the
secrets-in-logs guard. The module does not import `crate::ignore` at all, and its
header documents its six checks and a DRY vocabulary commitment while saying nothing
about the hatch — an unreviewed inconsistency, not a considered exception.

**Singleton, not an example.** Five modules consume `is_lazy_reason` from the canonical
`ignore.rs` — `ts_metric_naming`, `metric_labels`, `cite_extract`, `dashboard_panels`,
`alert_rules`. A crate-wide grep for bare-substring hatch forms returns exactly one hit.
The fix is therefore "import what this crate already imports five times", not "audit the
crate's hatches".

**Ladder inversion is the headline**: no hatch at all in `ts_retained_credentials.rs:43`
by deliberate design; enforced ≥10-char justification in dashboards and alert rules;
**bare marker in the guard covering passwords, tokens and keys in logs.**

**Cause is a missed migration, not a priorities gap** (@observability, verified):
`metric_labels.rs:4` is a "Verbatim port per @observability commitment #13" whose `:13`
enumerates the hatch semantics explicitly. The compliant modules inherited the
discipline from a port that had to spell out escape-hatch semantics to port them;
`rust_log_secrets` never went through that forcing function. Writing it as a priorities
story would be wrong.

**Adjacent, same three-line fix site**: `REDACTED` and `skip_all` are also bare
substring tests, so `tracing::info!("token={}", token); // not REDACTED yet` passes.

**Owner**: security for the policy, guard-family owner for the change. **To be
scheduled — no slug.**

### S18 — `cite_extract`'s `IN_SCOPE_DIRS` is narrower than the property both its guards enforce

`crates/dt-guard/src/cite_extract.rs` declares `IN_SCOPE_DIRS = ["docs/runbooks", ".claude/skills"]`,
and its own comment says *"Doc trees the new guards walk. Single source of truth — both guards
consume identical scope."* So **`cite-no-line-numbers` AND `cite-symbol-resolves` are both scoped to
those two trees**, while the properties they enforce — a line cite rots on any edit above it, a
symbol cite rots on rename — are not specific to those trees at all.

**This is a different failure from S16/S17 above, and the section predicate needs widening to cover
it.** S16/S17 are *path absent* — the root resolves to nothing and the guard scans an empty set.
Here the root resolves fine and the guard passes honestly; the property simply is not enforced
outside two directories. Extend the predicate to: *a guard's scope is an input; it must be asserted
present **and** justified against the property the guard enforces. Present-but-narrower-than-its-
premise is the silent case, because the guard reports clean and its scope is invisible from the
document it is not reading.*

**Measured 2026-09-07, both legs:**

- **Line-cite leg.** `docs/runbooks/` + `.claude/skills/` — zero bare line-cites; the guard works and
  holds its trees clean. `docs/specialist-knowledge/` — five INDEX files carry them
  (`auth-controller`, `dry-reviewer`, `infrastructure`, `observability`, `security`), ungoverned.
  Includes `docs/specialist-knowledge/security/INDEX.md`, which cites
  `crates/dt-guard/src/ts_retained_credentials.rs` by line plus two bare test-line cites — the most
  volatile kind, in the document every security reviewer is told to read first.
- **Symbol-cite leg** (found by @operations). 257 `file.rs:symbol` cites across 15 INDEX files, none
  resolved by anything. `docs/specialist-knowledge/operations/INDEX.md` has 18 symbol cites and
  **zero** line cites — clean on the first leg, wholly unguarded on the second. Worth stating plainly
  because reading only the line-cite measurement would license the conclusion "operations INDEX is
  fine", and it is not.

**Currently unexercised, and the entry should not imply otherwise.** Every symbol cite in the
security INDEX was checked and all resolve; there is no live rot today. This is a gap with no current
instance, which is a materially weaker claim than live staleness and is deliberately recorded as
such. *(Two earlier passes of that check reported nine stale and then one stale; both were artifacts
of the checker not replicating the guard's `BASENAME_SEARCH_ROOTS` fallback and then matching the
wrong `mod.rs`. Recorded because the same mistake is the obvious way to re-derive this wrongly.)*

**Why it is worth fixing rather than closing as won't-fix**: the affected files are navigation maps.
A stale cite there sends a reader somewhere confidently wrong, and the reader's next move is to trust
it rather than grep — the same "reads as coverage" failure ADR-0036 §11 names, one level up.

**Sequencing — the two legs are not one task.** Line-cites are a bounded mechanical sweep: five
files, delete or convert, then widen. Symbol-cites must each be *resolved* before widening, and any
already stale surface as failures rather than a clean cut-over. So: widen for line-cites first, then
resolve-and-widen for symbols. Widening `IN_SCOPE_DIRS` is not a config tweak — it reds five files
immediately, so sweep-then-widen is the order.

**Owner**: `infrastructure` / guard-family owner for the scope decision and machinery; policy input
from `security` + `observability` as the specialists whose INDEX files carry the most cites.
**Surfaced** 2026-09-07 by @paired-observability (line-cite leg) and @operations (symbol-cite leg) at
Gate 1/2 of `docs/devloop-outputs/2026-09-07-media-telemetry-deny-guard/`; measured and filed by
@security. **To be scheduled — no slug.**

## Validation Coverage Gap — NO env-test is type-checked below Layer 7 (owner: `infrastructure` for the machinery, consumer: `test`; found 2026-09-08 by @observability at Gate 2 of `docs/devloop-outputs/2026-09-08-mc-steer-client-to-edge-handler/`)

- [ ] **A cfg-gated test target can be syntactically broken while every cheap check in the tree reports clean.** `crates/env-tests/Cargo.toml` declares no default features (its own comment: *"No default features - tests require explicit --features flag"*), and every test target in the crate opens with `#![cfg(feature = ...)]`. So a featureless `cargo build -p env-tests --tests` / `cargo check -p env-tests --tests` **cfg-strips the whole target away and exits 0 having compiled none of it**.

  **Evidence, observed rather than reasoned**: against a tree where `crates/env-tests/tests/26_mh_quic.rs` failed to parse (`error: no rules expected keyword 'let'` under `cargo check -p env-tests --tests --features all`), the featureless form exited **0 in 0.13 seconds**. Review-protocol §Assertion Vacuity mechanism 5 — the subject ran where it could observe nothing and reported clean, indistinguishable from a real pass.

  **SIZED, so nobody re-derives it. The class is exactly the `env-tests` suite, and nothing else in the repo.** All **14 of 14** test targets in `crates/env-tests/tests/` carry the gate — `00_cluster_health.rs`, `01_mh_deployment_config.rs`, `10_auth_smoke.rs`, `20_auth_flows.rs`, `21_cross_service_flows.rs`, `22_mc_gc_integration.rs`, `23_meeting_creation.rs`, `24_join_flow.rs`, `25_auth_security.rs`, `26_mh_quic.rs`, `30_observability.rs`, `31_gc_telemetry.rs`, `32_media_metric_hygiene.rs`, `40_resilience.rs` — and the crate has no ungated test target. Every other `crates/*/tests/` and `crates/*/src/` was grepped for the same pattern: **no other crate uses it.**

  **Bigger than one file**: no env-test in this repository is type-checked by any layer below 7, so a syntax or type error anywhere in that suite is discoverable only with a live Kind cluster.

  **Narrower than a repo-wide policy question**: a single `--features all` scoped to the `env-tests` crate in the Layer 1 lanes would close it without touching how any other crate is built. The fix is plausibly small, which is an argument for **scheduling** it rather than letting it sit as an unbounded infra item.

  **Why the pipeline does not catch it.** Layer 1's lint lane is `scripts/lang/rust/lint.sh:7` (`cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets`) and its compile lane `scripts/lang/rust/compile.sh:18` (`cargo build --workspace`) — **neither passes a feature flag**. The only lane that compiles these targets is Layer 7's `scripts/layer7.sh:825` (`cargo test -p env-tests --features all`), which requires a live cluster.

  **The boundary of what IS covered, so nobody over-corrects.** `cargo test -p env-tests --lib` runs and is genuine: the lib target (`crates/env-tests/src/`, including `fixtures/metrics.rs`) has **no** `#![cfg]` gate, and it was observed passing 94 tests against the very tree whose `--tests` half would not compile. **The gap is specifically the `--tests` half.** A corollary worth keeping: decision logic pushed down into the unit-tested lib fixtures is *not* exposed to this gap — that placement is a mitigation for it, not a victim of it.

  **Candidate remedy, deliberately NOT pre-decided**: `--features all` on Layer 1's compile and lint lanes for this crate. Its owners must weigh build-time cost and whether `--features all` is the right selector versus an explicit feature list. Not attempted here.

  **Pre-existing, not introduced.** The 2026-09-08 devloop exposed this rather than causing it; the gap has existed since the `#![cfg]` gates landed. It is filed because a verification command that cannot see the file it verifies is worse than no command — it manufactures confidence, and it propagates: that devloop's own plan listed the featureless form *as* its verification step, so the next author would have inherited it.

## Devloop tooling assumes one commit per devloop; two-commit shapes break one gate and silently skip another

- [ ] **Two independent mechanisms assume a devloop is exactly one commit, and neither says so**
  (owner: `operations` for the skill's commit-shape guidance, `infrastructure` for the guard and
  hook machinery; surfaced 2026-09-07 in
  `docs/devloop-outputs/2026-09-07-media-telemetry-deny-guard/`). The devloop skill offers a
  multi-commit split so a risky change can be reverted without taking value-neutral refactors with
  it. Both mechanisms below assume that never happens.

  **(a) `validate-cross-boundary-scope` cannot pass a two-commit devloop — it reds.**
  `cross_boundary_scope.rs::fetch_diff_paths` resolves scope as working-tree-vs-HEAD when dirty,
  deliberately "narrower than the polyglot-pipeline merge-base … drift in THIS edit only". Once
  commit 1 lands, its files are in HEAD and absent from the active edit, so the plan lists files
  the edit does not touch and the guard emits `scope_drift_planned_untouched` for each. The plan
  describes the whole changeset; the active edit is half of it. There is no multi-commit
  provision, and the only exemption is the whole-file `docs/user-stories/*.md` carve-out.

  **(b) The Gate-2 hook goes quiet — the opposite failure, same premise.**
  `gate2_validate_commit` has two trigger conjuncts: a staged devloop `main.md` at
  `Phase=complete`, then a non-empty staged set after `gate2_is_excluded`. A code commit without
  `main.md` fails the first (matrix f); a `main.md`-only completion commit fails the second, since
  `docs/devloop-outputs/**` is excluded tree-wide (matrix c). Split a devloop so every commit lands
  in one cell and the local hook never demands a verdict. **Both cells are individually correct** —
  a `main.md`-only edit should not demand a fresh pipeline run, and ordinary commits are not
  devloop completions. Neither anticipated the split.

  **Not a security defect (@security, 2026-09-07).** `_gate2_binding.sh`'s header states the
  verdict is **anti-drift, not anti-forgery**, and the changeset digest is unkeyed, so a deliberate
  route-around is outside the stated threat model by construction. `.github/workflows/ci.yml` runs
  `layer-all.sh` from scratch and does not read the local verdict. **The residual is signal
  degradation, not enforcement loss** — do not escalate this as a merge-path bypass.

  **Cost of discovery**: (a) is silent until Gate 2, and `run-all` evaluates every layer — Layer 7
  had already spent **498 seconds** on env-tests and browser E2E against the live cluster before
  Layer 3 reported it.

  **Why it is worth recording rather than shrugging at**: a gap reachable only by deliberate action
  is uninteresting until the deliberate action becomes routine, and that transition is invisible
  from inside the control. Three people were designing two-commit shapes for good reasons on the
  evening this surfaced.

  **Options**: (a) teach the scope guard a multi-commit posture (accept the union of `HEAD^..HEAD`
  and working-tree when the plan is a superset); (b) drop the commit-split guidance from the skill
  and make two-step revert the documented compensating control; (c) exempt the plan-listing check
  when the branch carries commits sharing the devloop slug. **(b) is free and is what 2026-09-07
  did under time pressure; (a) is the one that restores the capability.** **Any fix must address
  both halves** — fixing only (a) would make two-commit devloops viable again *and* routine, which
  is precisely when (b) starts to matter. **To be scheduled — no slug.**

## Guard STATUS Attribution — `run-guards.sh` knows things its STATUS line doesn't say

- [ ] **A Layer-3 guard cannot self-declare an operator-lane precondition, and a violation's
  STATUS line names no guard.** Surfaced 2026-09-01 during Gate 1 of devloop
  `2026-09-01-release-premise-and-preflight-guards`, while establishing whether a new
  `dt-guard` subcommand could route its own "I could not find my inputs" result to the operator
  lane. It cannot, and establishing why turned up a second, adjacent gap. Both live at the same
  emission site in `scripts/guards/run-guards.sh`. **Neither is work for the surfacing diff** —
  they are behaviour changes to shared pipeline files that diff does not touch.

  **The measured mechanism** (recorded because two reviewers got it wrong in opposite directions
  before it was measured; see the §8 caveat repair in `docs/runbooks/devloop-validation.md`):
  whether a `STATUS=` line reaches Layer 3's aggregation depends on **who printed it**. Lines
  printed by `run-guards.sh` itself (`:156`, `:168`, `:253`) land on Layer 3's stdout, are
  collected by `tee_collect_statuses` (`scripts/lang/_common.sh:471-480`), and participate in
  both `aggregate_worst_status` and `worst_reason_for_status` (`_common.sh:396-407`, called at
  `:507`) — the latter taking the **first** pair matching the winning enum, which is what puts a
  cause on the stderr `LAYER=3 … REASON=` anchor. Lines printed by an individual guard
  subprocess are captured (`run-guards.sh:217`, `OUTPUT=$(…)`, the non-verbose default that
  `scripts/layer3.sh:27` uses) and re-emitted only when they match
  `VIOLATION|violation|ERROR|error|WARN`, capped at `head -5`. A guard's own `STATUS=` line
  matches none of those tokens and is silently dropped.

  **(a) Operator-lane self-declaration — a design conversation, not a patch.** A `2)` arm in
  `classify_guard_exit` echoing `STATUS=PRECONDITION_FAILURE REASON=guard-precondition-${GUARD_NAME}`
  would let any guard binary declare a precondition failure via exit 2, and it *would* work,
  because run-guards.sh's own echo sits outside the capture. **But it is a fourth hand-rolled
  `STATUS=` emission, and `run-guards.sh:285-296` records that as the standing trigger to revisit
  routing through `emit_status`** — which requires sourcing `lang/_common.sh`, rejected on coupling
  grounds per ADR-0015 §Pre-commit standalone use (run-guards.sh must stay standalone for
  pre-commit). So this is not "add an arm"; it trips a recorded architectural trigger. Size it as
  a design decision.

  **(b) Per-guard attribution for violations — a patch.** `run-guards.sh:253` emits a **fused
  constant**, `STATUS=FAIL REASON=guard-violations`, once when `FAILED_GUARDS > 0`, naming neither
  the guard nor its token, while the 124/137 arms carry `guard-timeout-${GUARD_NAME}`. **The
  asymmetry: the operator lane is attributable per-guard; the implementer lane is not.** A timeout
  tells you which guard; a violation tells you only that something violated, with the name
  surviving solely in the human `FAILED: <name>` line and the capped `head -5` re-emission.
  `FAILED_GUARD_NAMES` is already in scope at that site (printed at `:255-257`), so
  `guard-violations-${FAILED_GUARD_NAMES[0]}` for the single-guard case (fused constant retained
  as the multi-guard fallback) needs no new plumbing. **Do not flatten (a) and (b) into one size
  because they share a file and a function** — (a) is a design conversation, (b) is a patch.

  **The pin (b) needs, and the trap in specifying it.** `scripts/guards/run-guards.test.sh` is
  documented at `run-guards.sh:285-296` as the ONLY mechanical drift guard on this hand-copied exit
  ladder — and it is **blind to (b)**: `assert_status` is pure substring
  (`scripts/lang/_test_helpers.sh:45-47`), so appending `-<name>` leaves
  `STATUS=FAIL REASON=guard-violations` intact as a substring and `:135`/`:169` stay green through
  the change. **"Tighten to exact-match" is the wrong instruction** — followed literally it reds the
  multi-guard case while leaving the single-guard false-negative open. The pin is three parts:
  positive newline-anchored `$'REASON=guard-violations\n'` for the multi-guard fused form; positive
  prefix `"REASON=guard-violations-"` for the single-guard form, mirroring the existing
  truncated-needle convention at `:166`; and `assert_absent` with the **newline-anchored** needle
  for the single-guard case — a *bare* `assert_absent "REASON=guard-violations"` false-fails,
  because the suffixed form contains it as a substring. **Load-bearing caveat, stated with its
  reason so it survives the person who breaks it**: the suite captures via `out="$(cat "$RG_OUT")"`
  and command substitution strips *trailing* newlines, so newline-anchored needles work only while
  `:253` is not the last line of the capture. It isn't — `:254-258` print the header and name list
  immediately after. Reorder that block and the assertion breaks in a way that reads as a guard
  regression rather than a harness artifact.

  **Preferred fix for the pin: add the primitive, don't be clever at the call site.** The real gap
  is that `_test_helpers.sh` cannot express "this whole line equals X", which is why both the
  reviewer and the specialist proposed wrong assertions in consecutive messages while explicitly
  reasoning about substring semantics. Add `assert_status_line` / `assert_status_line_absent`
  mirroring the existing positive/negative pairing. **Purely additive — no existing call site
  changes behaviour**, which is the cheapest possible shape for a shared-SSoT change. An inline
  `grep -qx` was considered and rejected: a one-off idiom in a suite that speaks `assert_*`
  everywhere is a consistency cost paid by every future reader; the conclusion is that the idiom
  should become vocabulary, not be inlined.

  **Open scoping decision for whoever picks this up — size it deliberately.** Is the task "add the
  primitive", or "add the primitive **and** sweep the sites where the fixed-constant-vs-variable-suffix
  distinction is already load-bearing"? Only the second retires the trap rather than making it
  avoidable for future authors. Measured bounds so the choice is made from numbers: **286**
  `assert_status`/`assert_absent` invocations across **10** suites (`run-story` 138, `layer7` 56,
  `layer-all` 28, `run-guards` 16, `validate-subdomain-regex-sync` 16, `setup` 16,
  `audit-suppressions-check` 15, `_audit_gate` 1, `_changed_helpers` 0, plus the incoming
  `dev-web`); of those only **55** assert on a needle containing `STATUS=` or `REASON=` — the shape
  where the distinction can bite at all. The other 231 assert message fragments and markers where
  substring semantics is intended and whole-line matching would be actively wrong. The 55 concentrate in
  `layer7.test.sh` (**29 — over half**), then `run-guards` 9, `audit-suppressions-check` 8,
  `layer-all` 4, `validate-subdomain-regex-sync` 3, `run-story` 1, `_audit_gate` 1. Note the
  inversion: `run-story.test.sh` is 138 of the 286 assertions but only **1** of the 55, so the
  sweep's centre of mass is `layer7`, not `run-guards` — anchor the sizing there. The existing
  deliberate-prefix convention is **4 distinct needles**, all in `run-guards.test.sh` (the
  `guard-timeout-` / `guard-timeout-kill-` family). **This is a latent false-negative class, not a
  defect list: none of the 55 has been audited and none is claimed wrong.**

  **The sweep is not uniformly mechanical — positive and negative prefix assertions convert
  differently, and getting it wrong would introduce the exact defect this entry documents.** Of
  the 4 known-intentional prefix needles, **two are `assert_absent`**:
  `run-guards.test.sh:103` (`t124-no-old-fail-timeout`) and `:121` (`t137-no-old-fail-kill`) assert
  that `STATUS=FAIL REASON=guard-timeout-` / `-kill-` is **gone**. They pin ADR-0034 §9's
  2026-08-21 amendment, which moved timeout from `FAIL` to `PRECONDITION_FAILURE` leaving the
  REASON tokens byte-identical — so the enum is the *only* detectable signal of a regression, and
  these two are what detect it. Convert them mechanically and
  `assert_status_line_absent "STATUS=FAIL REASON=guard-timeout-"` asserts no line *equals* the bare
  prefix, which is trivially true forever (a real emission is always `…guard-timeout-<name>`). The
  assertion would pass permanently, stop pinning the amendment, and let a genuine regression sail
  through — a green test that has quietly stopped testing anything, i.e. the fix introducing the
  failure class it was meant to close. **Rule for the sweep: positive prefix assertions may convert
  to whole-line; negative prefix assertions may not.** The negative ones need either a prefix-aware
  absent primitive, or to stay on substring semantics deliberately with a comment saying why. Two
  of four known sites fall in the second category, so this is half the known-intentional set, not
  an edge case — and it is why the "add the primitive **and** sweep" option sits further from the
  cheap end than a raw site count implies.

  **Process note worth keeping, because it is this project's own failure mode pointed inward.**
  Six claims reached the reviewer during this Gate 1 as settled fact — a `kubectl` remedy command,
  a "live defect" framing, the `devloop-validation.md` §8 caveat, a proposed replacement for that
  caveat, a line citation, and an `assert_absent` proposal. Measuring each found **all six wrong**,
  including two of the reviewer's own, and every correction came from opening
  `scripts/lang/_common.sh`, `scripts/guards/run-guards.sh` and `scripts/lang/_test_helpers.sh`
  rather than from any agent's summary. A confidently relayed claim reads as a verified one; that
  is the same shape as a control that reads as coverage, which is what the surfacing devloop
  existed to close. The cheap countermeasure is the one that worked here: open the file before
  repeating the claim.

  **Owner**: operations. Provenance: Gate 1 of
  `docs/devloop-outputs/2026-09-01-release-premise-and-preflight-guards/main.md`, @operations +
  @observability, @team-lead ruling 2026-09-01 that all three items stay out of the surfacing diff.
  **To be scheduled — no slug.**

## Guard Coverage Gap — R-20 checks that a dashboard is REGISTERED, never that its group is LABELLED, so an unlabelled group is green and invisible (owner: `infrastructure` for the machinery; surfaced 2026-09-09 by @infrastructure as the owner-ACK condition on `infra/grafana/kustomization.yaml` in `docs/devloop-outputs/2026-09-09-media-dashboards-and-catalogs/`)

**Not the same defect as the R-20 entry under §Infrastructure Validation in Devloops** — that
one is a *parser* bug (line-oriented matching with no comment-stripping and no `- ` bullet
anchor, fixed 2026-09-05). This is a **scope** gap: the parser is now correct about the
question it asks, and the question is the wrong size. Filing separately so a future sweep of
the parser class does not read this as already closed.

`check_dashboard_coverage` (`crates/dt-guard/src/kustomize.rs`) compares the set of
`*.json` basenames in `infra/grafana/dashboards/` against the set declared in
`infra/grafana/kustomization.yaml`, bidirectionally. It never inspects `options.labels`.
The Grafana `kiwigrid/k8s-sidecar` (`infra/grafana/deployment.yaml`, `LABEL=grafana_dashboard`,
`LABEL_VALUE="1"`) mounts **only** ConfigMaps carrying that label. So a `configMapGenerator`
group that lists its files and omits

```yaml
    options:
      labels:
        grafana_dashboard: "1"
```

is registered, guarded, committed — and invisible in Grafana forever, with nothing red.

**Demonstrated, not asserted** (2026-09-09, against a copy of `infra/grafana/` at this commit):

- *Positive control*, so the negative is not vacuous — delete the `client-media.json` line
  from the generator and R-20 fires:
  `VIOLATION: infra/grafana/dashboards/client-media.json [dashboard_orphan] ... not in configMapGenerator`,
  `STATUS=FAIL`. The rule is live and reaching the file.
- *Negative control* — restore the line, delete only the `options.labels` block:
  **0 `dashboard_orphan` hits**, and `kubectl kustomize` renders
  `metadata: {name: grafana-dashboards-client, namespace: dark-tower-observability}` with
  **no labels at all**.

**The sibling failure is the same shape one hop downstream and has no guard either.** Because
`generatorOptions.disableNameSuffixHash: true` keeps generated names stable, changing a group's
contents does not alter the Grafana Deployment spec and does not roll the pod; and the sidecar
is a `METHOD: LIST` **initContainer** that lists once at pod start and exits. So `kubectl apply -k`
alone also yields a correct, correctly-labelled ConfigMap that Grafana never reads.
**The missing labels block and the missing `rollout restart` are one failure with two causes.**
Today both are covered only by prose (`docs/observability/dashboards.md` §Kubernetes, rewritten
in this devloop — it previously described auto-discovery that does not exist and told the reader
"no script edits required"). A doc is the weakest control available for a failure whose whole
character is that CI is green.

**Why this is not a predicate tweak.** `extract_declared_generator_files` is deliberately
**block-agnostic**: it flattens every `- ` bullet in the file with no notion of which generator
entry owns it. Asserting a label requires associating a `- name:` block with its `options.labels`
*and* its `files:` — a structure-aware matcher, not a new condition on the existing one. That
function is **shared** with the alert-rules loading check (`crates/dt-guard/src/alert_rules.rs`),
so changing its shape has a second consumer, and this rule class carries mandatory self-tests
(see the R-20 regression tests in `kustomize.rs`).

**Scope it wider than dashboards when acted on.** The general shape is *a generated ConfigMap is
invisible to its consumer without a selector label*, and there is at least one more instance:
the `prometheus-config` generator in `infra/kubernetes/observability/kustomization.yaml` carries
`options.labels` `app: prometheus` / `component: monitoring`. Fixing only the dashboards case is
the mechanism this file keeps recording — see the R-20 parser entry, where the prescribed sweep
found a fourth instance 90 lines from a fix already applied once.

**Ownership**: `infrastructure`. Per CLAUDE.md's guard-crate split, matcher implementations and
the shape of the constructs policy is expressed in are **machinery**; which label value is
required is content (`observability`). **Task-sized — to be scheduled, no slug.** Explicitly out
of scope for story task #22, whose changeset is dashboards and catalogs.
## Devloop & Team Structure Review (after ADR-0036 story 1)

**COLD-START BRIEF — read these before beginning; this section is the front door, the pointers below are the evidence.** This review is analysis + design, NOT a devloop: run it in a fresh host Claude session (read the sources, propose restructurings, likely a `/debate` on agent-scope consolidation, output an ADR); implement the ADR's changes via devloop afterward. Running the meta-review through the machinery it critiques is slow and circular.

- **Raw evidence, not summaries**: every `docs/devloop-outputs/*/main.md` from the ADR-0036 story-1 run carries a Gate-1 plan table, Gate-3 verdict table (finding counts, RESOLVED/CLEAR/DEFERRED, who caught what), and any escalation record — this is the primary data behind items (a)/(b). Per-task cost ledgers (attempts, usd, tokens, turns, api-minutes) are the `STORY_RUN: COST` lines in the run logs and the `cost-ledger.jsonl` files under the run dir (`~/.cache/devloop/story-runs/` on the host, or the in-container `/tmp/devloop-<slug>/story-runner/<story>/`); the story total was $5,682 / 2.8M output tokens / ~125 API-hours across 26 tasks.
- **The concentration finding (item b), stated once so it is not re-derived**: review value came almost entirely from reviewers who EXECUTE something — task 1 test's 16-mutation sweep catching an unreachable proof-of-trap; task 8 security's independent re-fetch + byte-diff of vendored crypto vectors and two correct escalations; task 11 DRY's exhaustive `PolicyRejection::ALL` walk finding a live defect; task 10 Gate-1 reviewers disproving an asserted (undenominatable) metric and an inverted semantic-guard check. Verdict-ceremony (ownership-lens discharge, ADDED-AT-GATE-3 rows, unanimous plan-confirmation rounds) produced most tokens and few shipped-byte changes. Gate 1 catches ran ~1-2/task vs Gate 3's ~3-5.
- **Related TODO entries that are inputs to this review** (do not treat as separate work): §Story Workflow Follow-ups (run-story v1 lessons, ADR-0035); the `DEVLOOP_TEST` seam-sentinel shared-home entry; the `list-tasks`-vs-`next` reopen-rewrite entries; the `producer | grep -q` pipefail class; and §"/close-story — worktree/branch-location robustness". Several are already-diagnosed mechanics the review should fold in rather than re-find.
- **Series context**: this was story 1 of an 8-story ADR-0036 arc (`docs/user-stories/2026-08-27-hear-yourself-through-handler.md` §series plan); the same devloop flow drives stories 2-8, so improvements compound. The `.claude/skills/devloop/`, `user-story/`, `close-story/` SKILLs and `.claude/agents/*.md` are the artifacts a restructuring edits.


- [ ] **Overall /devloop + team-structure review — speed and cost (owner: user + lead; timing: after `hear-yourself-through-handler` closes)**: parked by the user on 2026-09-02 mid-story to avoid process churn; discuss before story 2. Inputs to carry in:
  (a) **Measured cost shape** — per task: 1-4 full pipeline runs, 7-10 Gate-3 reviewers, 100-150 turns, $200-700; L7 dominates gate time (~8 min) and ran for diffs that could not affect it.
  (b) **Where review value concentrated** (evidence in story-1 main.md files): reviewers who EXECUTE — task 1 test's 16-mutation sweep catching an unreachable proof-of-trap branch; task 8 security's independent re-fetch/byte-diff of the vendored sframe-wg vectors and two correct escalations; task 11 DRY's exhaustive `PolicyRejection::ALL` walk catching a live defect; task 10 Gate-1 reviewers disproving an asserted metric (no denominator) and an inverted semantic-guard check. Verdict-ceremony (ownership-lens discharge, ADDED-AT-GATE-3 classification rows, plan-confirmation rounds that were unanimous rubber stamps 4/5 times) produced most tokens and few shipped-byte changes.
  (c) **Candidate restructurings**: risk-tier tasks (docs/guard-only vs single-crate vs cross-service) selecting reviewer count and gate depth; change-scoped Layer 7; one pipeline authority instead of devloop-Gate-2 + runner both running everything; strong-model plans / low-power implementers (industry pattern) — plan and review at high capability, mechanical implementation cheap; FEWER AGENTS WITH LARGER SCOPES — current 15 specialist scopes are narrow enough that cross-boundary choreography (co-signs, trailers, conditional adds) is a major turn sink.
  (d) **Semantic-guard rework**: in practice the teammate drifts beyond checks.md (invented `[meaning-drift-in-comments]` tag task 9; authored an inverted check at task 10 Gate 1; CLEAR on ~every task). Preferred shape: per-check scripted model calls (check text + diff -> FIRING/CLEAR + line cite) emitting a guard STATUS line — infrastructure, not a colleague. A prior attempt at in-devloop scripted model calls was unreliable; revisit on the run-story.sh substrate (headless `claude -p` per bounded prompt with exit-code discipline is now proven by the story runner).
  (f) **Terminal-phase recovery — commit-intent checkpoint + model-free finisher**: ~3 of the first 14 story-1 tasks died AFTER Gate 3 closed (CLI core dump at teardown, container PID exhaustion, quota), and recovery each time was a full devloop respawn re-hydrating a 100-turn transcript to run a gate and type git commit. Cheap shape: at Gate-3 close the devloop writes a machine-readable commit-intent (message, trailers, slug, expected file list — the task-14 escalation JSON already carried exactly this by hand); run-story.sh gains a --finish lane that with NO model run re-runs the gate, and if green stages exactly the intent's files (staged-index check), commits with the recorded message/trailers, and dt-story-completes with the slug; any mismatch refuses and falls back to resume. Safe because the intent replays a decision the review already made and the gate re-runs before commit. Complements --revalidate (committed-but-gate-red) by covering reviewed-but-uncommitted.
  (g) **Interactive-rescue lane for stuck headless tasks**: after N headless escalations on one task, drop to an interactive devloop instead of another headless attempt — `devloop.sh <slug>` (interactive attach) + `/devloop --continue=<task-slug>`; without DEVLOOP_HEADLESS the Lead asks the human in-session instead of escalating, converting each "human decision owed" into a conversation turn (task 24 burned four headless sessions re-deriving state that two interactive answers would have settled). Better shape (user, 2026-09-08): a `run-story.sh --interactive` retry mode — the runner spawns `claude` ATTACHED to the operator's TTY (same prompt/--continue, DEVLOOP_HEADLESS unset for that spawn only, no stream-json redirect, no task timeout, Stop-hook relaxed), waits for the human to exit, then falls through to the UNCHANGED gate/commit-detection/complete/escalate machinery — the runner does not care how the devloop concluded, only about HEAD movement and gate rc. Cost ledger records kind=interactive. Consider auto-suggesting it after the second escalation of one task.
  (e) **Runner/guard interaction fixes already landed mid-story** (fold into the review rather than redo): --revalidate/--restart flags, effective-diff-all-exempt scope-guard rule, .devloop-escalation.json exemption, tracked-files-only subdomain sweep, per-instance env-config discovery.

## /close-story — worktree/branch-location robustness (2026-09-14)

- [ ] **`/close-story` does not state or verify it is running on the story branch, and its narrow git scope silently ignores unrelated dirty state (owner: operations/tooling)**: observed at ADR-0036 story-1 close. The skill commits reflection + pushes the CURRENT branch + opens a PR via `gh pr create --head $(git branch --show-current)` — correct only when invoked from the worktree holding `feature/<story-slug>` (which does carry a proper GitHub origin, so push/PR work there). Run from the wrong checkout it would push the wrong branch. Two small hardenings: (a) Phase 1 verify the current branch matches the story's `feature/<slug>` (or at least warn if not), so a mis-located invocation fails loudly instead of pushing the wrong branch; (b) Phase 3's stage-only-INDEX+devloop-outputs scope means unrelated uncommitted files (e.g. a crash-left `oom` artifact, or a standalone non-manifest devloop's work still uncommitted) are neither swept nor flagged — the `git status --short` safety check should surface them as a caution in the Phase 5 report rather than leave the operator to notice. Neither is a data-loss bug (scope is deliberately narrow), but both are "silent when it should be loud" ergonomics. Not blocking; fold into the parked devloop/team-structure review or a small tooling devloop.
